corp-management.title: Management, leadership and workplace communication
corp-management.description: Chapter-by-chapter people leadership: becoming a manager, 1:1s, feedback and coaching, goals and performance, motivating and leading teams, workplace communication, and decisions and leadership styles.

courses.title: Ch 1 · From individual contributor to manager
courses.summary: What managers actually do, how to delegate well, how to manage your time and priorities, and a plan for your first 90 days leading a team.
outcomes: Learners can describe the shift from doing to enabling
Learners can choose what and how to delegate
Learners can prioritise with the Eisenhower matrix
Learners can write a 30-60-90 day plan as a new manager

scenes.text: Priya, the team's best engineer, is promoted to manager. She keeps taking the hardest tickets herself.
Six weeks later her team is blocked, waiting for her reviews, and she's working till midnight.
Her mentor says: 'Your output is now your team's output.'

steps.title: The big shift
steps.body: As an individual contributor (IC), success = **your** work. As a manager, success = **your team's results and growth**. Your main tools become: setting direction, hiring and developing people, removing blockers, making decisions, and communicating up, down and across.

steps.title: Core responsibilities
steps.body:
- **Clarity:** goals, priorities, roles
- **People:** hiring, 1:1s, feedback, coaching, growth, recognition
- **Execution:** plans, risks, removing blockers, quality
- **Communication:** updates to stakeholders, context to the team
- **Culture:** safety, fairness, standards

steps.title: Solved example: Priya's reset
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Stop owning critical-path tickets; pair on hard problems instead.
**Step 2:** Weekly 1:1s with each person.
**Step 3:** Review rota so reviews aren't all on her.
**Step 4:** Block 'maker time' for strategy and stakeholder work.
**Result:** team throughput rises; she works normal hours.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Being the 'super-IC' bottleneck.
- Avoiding hard conversations to stay liked.
- Managing everyone the same way regardless of experience.

activity.prompt: IC habit or manager habit?

items.text: Taking the hardest task yourself every time
Holding weekly 1:1s
Removing blockers for the team
Rewriting team members' work at night
Explaining the 'why' behind priorities
Measuring your day by your own commits

quiz.why: A manager's output is mainly the team's results and growth. Meetings and personal tasks are only means.
Super-IC managers, who keep doing the work themselves, often become bottlenecks because everything waits for them.

quiz.q: Which is a core manager responsibility?
quiz.why: Giving feedback and coaching is a core manager responsibility, as it develops people. Hiding problems or avoiding decisions is not.
Managing everyone identically ignores their different skill and experience levels. Good managers adapt to the person.

quiz.q: Blocking 'maker time' as a manager helps with:
quiz.why: Blocking 'maker time' gives managers uninterrupted time for strategy and planning work.

story.title: I'll just do it, it's faster

scenes.text: Arun says delegating takes longer than doing it himself.
By the third time, his team member does it faster than him — and Arun has time for planning.

steps.title: What to delegate
steps.body: Delegate: recurring tasks, tasks that grow someone's skills, work others can do 80% as well. Keep: confidential people issues, final accountability, tasks only you are authorised to do.

steps.title: Levels of delegation
steps.body:
1) **Do as I say** (follow instructions)
2) **Research and report** options
3) **Recommend** — I decide
4) **Decide and tell me**
5) **Decide; no need to tell me**
Match the level to the person's skill and the task's risk; increase over time.

steps.title: Solved example: a clear hand-off
steps.body: Arun to Meena: 'Please own the weekly client report from next week (**what**). It helps the client track SLAs (**why**). Draft it by Thursday 4 pm (**when**); use last month's template (**how/resources**). You decide the format; send me the draft the first two weeks, then just send it (**level 3 → 4**). Ask me anytime.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Dumping' tasks without context or authority.
- Taking work back at the first mistake.
- Delegating only boring work, never growth opportunities.
- Delegating responsibility but not accountability — you still own the outcome.

activity.prompt: Order the delegation levels from least to most autonomy.

options: What, why, when, resources and authority level
quiz.why: A good hand-off covers what, why, when, the resources and the level of authority. A deadline alone leaves too much unclear.
When delegating, accountability stays with the manager, because you still own the outcome. Only the task is handed over.
Delegating only boring tasks misses growth opportunities. People develop by taking on meaningful work.

quiz.q: Taking work back after the first mistake:
quiz.why: Taking work back after the first mistake undermines learning and trust. Coach instead.

options: Brand-new hire on a high-risk task
quiz.why: 'Decide and tell me' suits an experienced person on a moderate-risk task. A new hire on a high-risk task needs more direction.

scenes.text: Rakesh spends his day on urgent emails and pings; the hiring plan due next week isn't started.
He draws four boxes and sorts his work.

steps.title: Eisenhower matrix
steps.body:
- **Urgent + important:** do now (production incident, deadline today).
- **Important, not urgent:** **schedule** — planning, hiring, coaching, learning (where managers create most value).
- **Urgent, not important:** delegate or batch (many pings, some requests).
- **Neither:** drop.

steps.title: Practical habits
steps.body:
- Weekly planning: top 3 outcomes.
- Calendar blocks for important-not-urgent work.
- Batch email/chat at set times.
- Say 'not now' with a date: 'I can look at this Thursday.'

steps.title: Solved example: sort Rakesh's list
steps.body: Incident at a key client → **Do**. Hiring plan due next week → **Schedule** (2 h tomorrow). Request to forward a deck → **Delegate**. Reading every all-company thread → **Drop/skim**. Coaching a struggling report → **Schedule** this week.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Living in the urgent box.
- Never protecting time for 1:1s and planning.

activity.prompt: Place each task in the Eisenhower matrix.

items.text: Customer-facing outage
Quarterly team planning
Collating weekly status numbers
Scrolling an unrelated channel
Career conversation with a report
Booking a meeting room

quiz.q: Important but not urgent work should be:
quiz.why: Important but not urgent work should be scheduled, so it gets protected time before it becomes urgent.

quiz.q: Most managerial value usually sits in:
quiz.why: Most managerial value sits in the important, not urgent quadrant, such as planning and people development.
Urgent but not important tasks should be delegated or batched, which reduces interruptions.
Saying 'not now' well includes a concrete alternative time, which keeps a respectful boundary.
Plan your week around your top 3 outcomes, to keep focus.

lessons.title: Your first 90 days as a manager

scenes.text: Kiran is promoted to lead the team she was part of — including her close friend.
She writes a 30-60-90 plan to start well.

steps.title: 30-60-90 plan
steps.body:
- **Days 1–30: Listen and learn.** 1:1 with each person (goals, frustrations, ideas), meet stakeholders, understand metrics and processes.
- **Days 31–60: Small wins and clarity.** Share what you heard, agree team priorities and working norms, fix 1–2 quick pain points.
- **Days 61–90: Direction.** Set goals/OKRs, development plans, rhythms (1:1s, reviews), and a roadmap.

steps.title: Managing former peers and friends
steps.body: Acknowledge the change openly: 'Our relationship changes a bit — I'll be fair to everyone, and I'll still value your honesty.' Avoid favouritism (and its appearance) in assignments, ratings and information.

steps.title: Solved example: first 1:1 questions
steps.body:
- What's going well, and what's frustrating?
- What should I keep, stop, start?
- How do you like to receive feedback?
- What are your career goals for the next 1–2 years?
- What do you need from me?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing everything in week one.
- Gossiping with old friends about team members.
- Not asking your own manager what success looks like.

activity.prompt: New manager's first 30 days
items: Met my manager to agree success criteria
Read team metrics and recent incidents

quiz.why: In days 1–30, listen and learn so you understand the team before making changes. Reorganising or firing early is premature.

options: Acknowledge the change and be visibly fair
quiz.why: With former peers, acknowledge the change and be visibly fair. Pretending nothing changed or favouring friends damages trust.

options: What do you need from me?
quiz.why: 'What do you need from me?' opens dialogue in a first 1:1. Questions about complaints or salary don't.
Ask your own manager what success looks like, so you are aligned on expectations.
Quick wins in days 31–60 build credibility and momentum.

questions.q: A manager's success is measured mostly by:
questions.why: A manager's success is measured mostly by team outcomes, not emails or personal tasks.

questions.q: Eisenhower 'neither urgent nor important':
questions.why: In the Eisenhower matrix, tasks that are neither urgent nor important should be dropped.

questions.q: First 30 days as a new manager:
questions.why: In the first 30 days as a new manager, listen and learn before changing things.

questions.q: Which should usually NOT be delegated?
questions.why: Confidential people decisions are part of the manager's role and shouldn't be delegated. Data collation, reports and meeting notes can be.

questions.q: 'Recommend; I decide' is delegation level:
questions.why: 'Recommend; I decide' is the middle delegation level, level 3, where the report proposes and the manager decides.

questions.q: Planning and coaching are typically:
questions.why: Planning and coaching are important but not urgent, so you schedule them.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Delegation moves accountability to the team member. Reason (R): Managers remain responsible for outcomes.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: managers remain responsible for outcomes, so delegation doesn't move accountability to the team member.

questions.q: A good hand-off includes all EXCEPT:
questions.why: A good hand-off shares the purpose, the what, when and authority level. Hiding the purpose is what it should not do.

questions.q: Super-IC behaviour causes:
questions.why: Super-IC behaviour causes bottlenecks and burnout, since the manager becomes a single point everything depends on.

questions.q: Case: New manager's friend expects the best projects. Best response?
options: Explain assignments are based on fit and fairness; offer growth openly
questions.why: Explain that assignments are based on fit and fairness, and offer growth openly. Giving a friend everything or avoiding them is unfair.

questions.q: Case: You spend 80% of time in urgent pings. Best change?
options: Batch messages, delegate, block time for important work
questions.why: With 80% of time in urgent pings, batch messages, delegate and block time for important work. Working weekends or answering faster doesn't fix it.

questions.q: Case: A junior made an error on a delegated report. Best response?
options: Review together, explain, keep the task with closer check-ins
questions.why: Review the error together, explain, and keep the task with closer check-ins. Taking it back forever or criticising publicly harms learning.

questions.q: Case: Day 10 as manager — you want to change the team's process. Best?
options: Listen first; propose changes after understanding why it exists
questions.why: On day 10, listen first and propose changes after understanding why the process exists. Changing it today may remove something that serves a purpose.

questions.q: Which BEST shows you've moved from IC to manager mindset?
options: Measuring your week by team blockers removed and people grown
questions.why: Measuring your week by team blockers removed and people grown shows a manager mindset focused on leverage. Hours, tickets or code lines are IC measures.

questions.q: Which delegation level for an experienced engineer on a low-risk, recurring task?
questions.why: For an experienced engineer on a low-risk, recurring task, 'decide; no need to report' fits, since it gives maximum autonomy.

courses.title: Ch 2 · 1:1s, feedback and coaching
courses.summary: Running useful one-on-ones, giving feedback with the SBI model, coaching with GROW, and receiving feedback and recognising people well.
outcomes: Learners can run a 1:1 that the team member owns
Learners can give specific, behaviour-based feedback with SBI
Learners can coach using GROW questions
Learners can receive feedback without defensiveness and give meaningful recognition

scenes.text: Deepak's 1:1s are just task status. His best engineer resigns, saying she 'never felt heard'.
He redesigns his 1:1s around the person, not the tasks.

steps.title: Purpose
steps.body: A 1:1 is **the team member's meeting**: their priorities, blockers, growth, wellbeing and feedback both ways. Status belongs in standups or dashboards.

steps.title: A simple structure (30 min, weekly or fortnightly)
steps.body:
1) Their topics first (shared running doc)
2) Blockers and support needed
3) Feedback both ways
4) Growth/career (at least monthly)
5) Actions and owners

steps.title: Solved example: good questions
steps.body:
- 'What's on your mind this week?'
- 'What's slowing you down that I can remove?'
- 'What's one thing I could do better as your manager?'
- 'Which work energised you recently?'
- 'How are you, really — workload okay?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cancelling 1:1s whenever busy — signals people aren't a priority.
- Talking 80% of the time.
- No notes or follow-up on promised actions.

activity.prompt: 1:1 health check
items: Recurring 1:1 on the calendar with each report
Shared agenda document they can add to
They speak more than I do
I ask for feedback on myself
Actions are written and followed up

options: The team member's priorities, growth and blockers
quiz.why: A 1:1 is mainly for the team member's priorities, growth and blockers. It is their meeting, not a status report.
Frequent cancellations signal that people aren't a priority, even if you meant no harm.

quiz.q: Who should talk more in a 1:1?
quiz.why: The team member should talk more in a 1:1, while the manager listens.
Career topics should come up regularly, for example monthly, not only at appraisal or exit.
Status updates belong in standups or dashboards, which frees 1:1 time for people topics.

scenes.text: Rina's manager tells her, 'You're not a team player.' She has no idea what to change.
A different manager uses SBI — and Rina knows exactly what to do.

steps.title: SBI model
steps.body:
The **Situation–Behaviour–Impact** model (popularised by the Center for Creative Leadership):
- **Situation:** when and where
- **Behaviour:** what the person did or said (observable, not labels)
- **Impact:** the effect on you, the team, the customer
Then invite their view and agree a next step.

steps.title: Solved example: corrective feedback
steps.body:
**Label (unhelpful):** 'You're not a team player.'
**SBI:** 'In Tuesday's sprint review (S), you interrupted Aman three times while he presented (B). He stopped sharing his ideas and we lost his input on the design (I). What was going on for you? Next time, could you note questions and ask at the end?'

steps.title: Solved example: positive feedback
steps.body: 'In yesterday's client call (S), you summarised the three open risks and owners in two minutes (B). The client said it was the clearest update they'd had, and we got sign-off a week early (I). Please keep doing that in every call.'

steps.title: Timing and ratio
steps.body: Give feedback **soon**, **privately** for corrective feedback, and much more often for things done well. Make it about behaviour, never personality.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The 'feedback sandwich' that hides the message.
- Saving feedback for the annual review.
- Using 'always/never'.

activity.prompt: Label each part of the SBI statement.
pairs: '…you presented the budget without the cost breakdown…'
'…so the CFO couldn't approve it and we lost a week.'
'Let's add a breakdown slide by Thursday.'

quiz.why: SBI stands for Situation, Behaviour, Impact, a feedback model.

quiz.q: Which is a behaviour (not a label)?
options: 'You arrived 20 minutes late to the client call'
quiz.why: 'You arrived 20 minutes late to the client call' is an observable behaviour. 'Lazy', 'unprofessional' and 'bad attitude' are labels.
Corrective feedback works best soon after the event and in private. Public or late feedback is less relevant and less respectful.
After SBI, invite their perspective, to make it a dialogue rather than a verdict.
Positive feedback should be specific and frequent, so it reinforces the behaviour you want.

story.title: Just tell me what to do

scenes.text: Sahil keeps bringing problems to his manager expecting answers.
His manager starts asking questions instead — and Sahil starts solving problems himself.

steps.title: The GROW model
steps.body:
Developed by Sir John Whitmore and colleagues:
- **Goal:** What do you want to achieve?
- **Reality:** What's happening now? What have you tried?
- **Options:** What could you do? What else?
- **Will (way forward):** What will you do, by when? How committed are you (1–10)?

steps.title: Solved example: a coaching conversation
steps.body:
**G:** 'What would a good outcome be for the vendor delay?' → 'Delivery by the 20th.'
**R:** 'Where are things now?' → 'They're short of testers.'
**O:** 'What options do you see?' → 'Lend our tester; cut scope; escalate.'
**W:** 'Which will you do and when?' → 'Offer our tester for 3 days and agree scope by Friday.'

steps.title: Coach vs tell
steps.body: **Tell** when there's a crisis, a safety issue, or the person is new and lacks basic knowledge. **Coach** when the person has some capability and the goal is growth and ownership.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leading questions that are disguised instructions.
- Skipping 'Will' — no commitment, no action.
- Coaching during an emergency.

activity.prompt: Match the question to the GROW stage.
pairs: 'What do you want to achieve by month-end?'
'What will you do first, and by when?'
'On a scale of 1–10, how committed are you?'

quiz.why: GROW was developed by Sir John Whitmore and colleagues.
In GROW, R stands for Reality, asking about the current situation.

options: The person has capability and growth is the goal
quiz.why: Coach rather than tell when the person has capability and growth is the goal. Use telling for day one, safety issues or emergencies.
Skipping the 'Will' stage leaves no commitment to act, so nothing may change.
Good coaching questions are open-ended, which prompts exploration. Yes/no, leading or accusatory questions don't.

scenes.text: Neha's team survey says she 'doesn't recognise effort'. Her first reaction is to explain why they're wrong.
Instead she thanks them, asks for examples and changes one habit.

steps.title: Receiving feedback
steps.body: 1) **Listen** fully. 2) **Thank** the person — it took courage. 3) **Clarify** with examples. 4) **Reflect** before responding. 5) **Act** and tell them what you changed. You don't have to agree with everything, but you do have to consider it.

steps.title: Recognition that lands
steps.body: Specific (what and why it mattered), timely, sincere, and fair across the team. Some people like public praise; others prefer private notes — ask. Recognise effort and learning, not just big wins.

steps.title: Solved example: specific recognition
steps.body:
Generic: 'Great job, team!'
Specific: 'Farhan, staying calm during last night's outage and writing clear updates every 30 minutes kept the client informed and avoided an escalation. Thank you.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Defensiveness: 'Yes, but…'.
- Recognising only the loudest people.
- Asking for feedback and never acting on it.

a.text: A team member says, 'In meetings, you often cut people off.' Your response?

choices.label: 'That's not true, I just keep meetings efficient.'
'Thank you for telling me. Can you give me an example?'

b.text: They go quiet. Months later you learn others felt the same. Try again?

choices.label: Go back, apologise, and ask for examples

c.text: They share two examples. What next?

choices.label: Commit to a change and ask them to flag it if it happens again
Say thanks and change nothing

d.text: A month later the team says meetings feel more open. You thank them for the feedback publicly.

e.text: People stop giving you feedback. Lesson: act on what you hear.

quiz.why: When receiving feedback, first listen fully to understand it. Defending or countering shuts the conversation down.
Effective recognition is specific and timely, so the person knows what was valued.

options: Act and tell them what changed
quiz.why: After feedback, act on it and tell them what changed. This closes the loop.
'Yes, but…' signals defensiveness, since it dismisses what came before the 'but'.
People differ, so ask the person's preference about public or private praise.

questions.q: SBI 'I' stands for:
questions.why: In SBI, I stands for Impact, the effect of the behaviour.

questions.q: GROW 'O' stands for:
questions.why: In GROW, O stands for Options. The stages are Goal, Reality, Options and Will.

questions.q: Whose meeting is a 1:1?
questions.why: A 1:1 is the team member's meeting, so they own the agenda.

questions.q: Which is behaviour-based feedback?
options: 'You missed the 5 pm deadline twice this week'
questions.why: 'You missed the 5 pm deadline twice this week' is specific, observable behaviour. 'Careless' or 'don't care' are labels.

questions.q: Coaching suits:
questions.why: Coaching suits building ownership in capable people. Day-one hires, emergencies and safety issues need direction.

questions.q: Recognition should be:
questions.why: Recognition should be specific, because it shows what was valued and lands better.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The feedback sandwich always works best. Reason (R): Hiding the main point between praise can blur the message.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: the feedback sandwich can hide the main point between praise and blur the message.

questions.q: 'What have you tried so far?' is GROW stage:
questions.why: 'What have you tried so far?' explores the current situation, so it is the Reality stage of GROW.

questions.q: A 1:1 dominated by task status:
questions.why: A 1:1 dominated by task status misses growth and wellbeing topics. Status can be shared elsewhere.

questions.q: Case: Team member's code reviews are harsh and others avoid asking him. Best SBI?
options: 'In last week's reviews (S), comments like "this is junk" (B) made two juniors stop asking you (I). What's your view?'
questions.why: The SBI statement names the situation, the behaviour (the specific comment) and its impact, then invites his view. 'You're toxic' is a label, and ignoring it lets it continue.

questions.q: Case: During a production outage, a junior asks what to do. Best approach?
options: Tell clearly now; coach in the retro later
questions.why: In a production outage, tell clearly now and coach in the retro later. Crisis calls for direction, not 20 minutes of questions.

questions.q: Case: You receive feedback you disagree with. Best?
options: Thank, ask for examples, reflect, then respond thoughtfully
questions.why: Thank them, ask for examples, reflect, then respond thoughtfully. Arguing or retaliating wastes useful information.

questions.q: Which combination best improves 1:1s?
options: Shared agenda, their topics first, regular growth talk, written actions
questions.why: Good 1:1s have a shared agenda, put their topics first, discuss growth regularly and record actions. Manager monologues, status-only or cancelled meetings don't.

questions.q: Why is specific recognition more motivating than generic praise?
options: It shows you noticed what mattered and reinforces that exact behaviour
questions.why: Specific recognition shows you noticed what mattered and reinforces that exact behaviour. Generic praise doesn't tell people what to repeat.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Goals, OKRs and performance
courses.summary: Writing SMART goals, setting OKRs, handling performance conversations and underperformance fairly, and reducing bias in reviews and calibration.
outcomes: Learners can rewrite vague goals as SMART goals
Learners can write objectives with measurable key results
Learners can run a fair underperformance process
Learners can spot and reduce common rating biases

scenes.text: A support team's goal is 'improve customer satisfaction'. At year end, nobody knows if they did.
Next year they write it SMART.

steps.title: SMART
steps.body:
- **Specific:** what exactly
- **Measurable:** how you'll know
- **Achievable:** stretching but realistic
- **Relevant:** linked to team/company priorities
- **Time-bound:** by when

steps.title: Solved example: rewrite
steps.body:
Vague: 'Improve customer satisfaction.'
SMART: 'Raise CSAT for chat support from 78% to 85% by 31 March by cutting first-response time from 6 to 2 minutes and publishing 20 new help articles.'

steps.title: Solved example: a personal growth goal
steps.body:
Vague: 'Get better at presenting.'
SMART: 'Present the team's monthly update to leadership in 3 of the next 4 months, with feedback scores of 4/5 or higher, after completing the internal presentation workshop by 15 May.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Activities instead of outcomes ('hold 10 meetings').
- Too many goals — aim for 3–5.
- Goals no one revisits until appraisal.

activity.prompt: SMART or not?

items.text: Reduce invoice errors from 4% to 1% by Q3
Be more proactive
Launch the Hindi app version to 100% of users by 30 June
Work harder on quality
Close 12 enterprise deals worth ₹6 crore this financial year

quiz.why: In SMART, M stands for Measurable.
'Be more proactive' is vague, so it fails mainly on being specific and measurable.
A good number of goals is 3 to 5, which keeps focus.
Goals should focus on outcomes, the results achieved, not just hours, meetings or activity.
In SMART, T stands for Time-bound, meaning there is a deadline.

scenes.text: A product team ships 40 features in a quarter but user retention doesn't change.
They switch to OKRs focused on outcomes.

steps.title: Objectives and Key Results
steps.body:
- **Objective:** qualitative, inspiring direction ('Make onboarding effortless for new users').
- **Key Results (2–5):** measurable outcomes that prove progress ('Day-7 retention from 32% to 40%', 'Time to first value under 5 minutes', 'Onboarding support tickets down 30%').
- **Initiatives:** the projects you'll do to move the KRs (not KRs themselves).

steps.title: Committed vs aspirational
steps.body: **Committed** OKRs are expected to be fully met. **Aspirational** (stretch) OKRs aim high; achieving ~70% can be a good result. Be clear which is which, and don't tie stretch OKRs directly to individual ratings, or people will sandbag.

steps.title: Solved example: fix a bad KR
steps.body:
Bad KR: 'Launch new onboarding flow' (that's an initiative/output).
Better KR: 'Increase onboarding completion from 55% to 75%.'
Scoring: completion reaches 70% → (70−55)/(75−55) = **0.75**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing tasks as KRs.
- Too many OKRs.
- Setting and forgetting — review weekly or fortnightly.

activity.prompt: KR: increase NPS from 30 to 50. You reach 44. Score (0–1, two decimals)?

quiz.why: A Key Result must be measurable, so progress can be proved. A task or vague aim isn't a KR.
'Launch feature X' is an output, usually an initiative rather than a Key Result. A KR measures the outcome it should achieve.
Typically 2 to 5 key results per objective keeps it focused.
Aspirational OKRs scored around 70% can be a good result, since stretch goals aren't expected to be fully met.
OKRs should be reviewed regularly, weekly or fortnightly, so you can steer. Annual-only review is too late.

scenes.text: Vivek receives a low rating at year-end — the first he's heard of any problem.
His new manager commits: 'No surprises, ever.'

steps.title: No surprises
steps.body: If someone is shocked by their review, the manager failed earlier. Give feedback continuously; reviews should summarise conversations already held.

steps.title: Fair underperformance process
steps.body:
1) **Diagnose:** skill, will, clarity, or circumstances (health, family, workload)?
2) **Clarify expectations** in writing with examples.
3) **Support:** training, pairing, resources, check-ins.
4) **Agree a time-bound plan** with measurable goals (a performance improvement plan, if used, must be genuine — a path to success, not a paper trail to exit).
5) **Review** regularly and document.
6) **Decide** fairly, following policy and law; involve HR.

steps.title: Solved example: diagnosis
steps.body:
Ankit's tickets are late. In the 1:1 you learn he was never trained on the new framework and his parent is in hospital.
**Actions:** training + pairing (skill); flexible hours/leave options (circumstances); revisit in 4 weeks with clear targets.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming poor performance = laziness.
- Vague expectations ('step up').
- Using a PIP as a formality for a decision already made.

activity.prompt: Order a fair underperformance process.
items: Diagnose the cause in a private conversation
Clarify expectations with examples, in writing
Make a fair decision with HR, following policy

quiz.why: A surprise low rating means feedback wasn't given earlier. Reviews should have no surprises.
The first step with underperformance is to diagnose the cause, before any PIP, pay cut or firing.

options: A real path to success with support
quiz.why: A genuine PIP is a real path to success with support. Using it as a paper trail to exit is unfair.
Underperformance can come from skill, will, clarity or circumstances. Diagnosing which one decides the response.
Expectations should be specific and written, so everyone knows what success looks like.

scenes.text: In calibration, one manager says, 'Ravi is just like me — sharp. Top rating.'
The HR partner asks: 'What evidence do we have?'

steps.title: Common biases
steps.body:
- **Recency:** last few weeks outweigh the year.
- **Halo/horns:** one strong trait (good or bad) colours everything.
- **Similarity/affinity:** favouring people like us.
- **Central tendency:** rating everyone average.
- **Leniency/strictness:** consistently too high/low.
- **Visibility bias:** remote or quiet workers under-rated.
- **Gender/caste/regional stereotypes:** unfair assumptions.

steps.title: Reducing bias
steps.body:
- Keep a running evidence log all year.
- Rate against written criteria, not people against each other's personalities.
- Use specific examples for every rating.
- In calibration, ask 'what's the evidence?' and compare similar roles.

steps.title: Solved example: challenge a rating
steps.body: 'Ravi is sharp' → 'Which outcomes against his goals support the top rating? He met 2 of 4 goals; Sneha met 4 of 4 working remotely. Let's re-check both against the criteria.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing reviews from memory in one evening.
- Ignoring quieter or remote contributors.
- Letting the loudest manager win calibration.

activity.prompt: Match the example to the bias.
pairs: Last month's mistake outweighs a great year
Great presenter, so assumed great at everything
Same college and hometown as the manager

quiz.why: Recency bias overweights recent events and underweights the rest of the year.
The best defence against bias is an evidence log against written criteria. Gut feeling or popularity invite bias.
Similarity bias favours people like the rater.
In calibration, ask 'What's the evidence?' to keep ratings fair.
Rating everyone 'average' is central tendency bias.

questions.q: SMART 'A' stands for:
questions.why: In SMART, A stands for Achievable, meaning realistic.

questions.q: OKR 'KR' must be:
questions.why: A Key Result must be measurable, to show progress.

questions.q: Recency bias:
questions.why: Recency bias overweights recent events when judging performance.

questions.q: First step with underperformance:
questions.why: The first step with underperformance is to diagnose the cause.

questions.q: 'Ship 10 features' as a KR is:
options: An output, better as an initiative
questions.why: 'Ship 10 features' is an output, which is better as an initiative. A KR should measure the outcome.

questions.q: Halo effect:
questions.why: The halo effect is when one good trait colours your overall view of a person.

questions.q: KR: churn from 8% to 4%. Achieved 5%. Score?
Assertion (A): Reviews should contain no surprises. Reason (R): Feedback should be continuous through the year.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: feedback should be continuous through the year, so the review contains no surprises.

questions.q: Which goal is SMART?
options: Cut onboarding time from 10 to 5 days by Q2
questions.why: 'Cut onboarding time from 10 to 5 days by Q2' is specific, measurable and time-bound. 'Be better' and 'try hard' are vague.

questions.q: Visibility bias affects:
questions.why: Visibility bias affects remote and quieter employees, because their work is less seen.

questions.q: Case: A report's work slipped after a family emergency. Best approach?
options: Discuss support/flexibility, adjust timelines, review later
questions.why: After a family emergency, discuss support or flexibility, adjust timelines and review later. An immediate PIP or public warning ignores the circumstances.

questions.q: Case: Stretch OKR tied to bonus; team sets easy targets. Problem?
options: Linking stretch OKRs to pay encourages sandbagging
questions.why: Linking stretch OKRs to pay encourages sandbagging, so teams set easy targets. Stretch goals work best separate from bonuses.

questions.q: Case: In calibration, a manager argues from personality, not results. Best intervention?
options: Ask for evidence against criteria and compare similar roles
questions.why: Ask for evidence against criteria and compare similar roles. Arguing from personality is bias.

questions.q: Which is the BEST KR for 'Delight first-time buyers'?
options: Repeat purchase within 30 days from 18% to 25%
questions.why: 'Repeat purchase within 30 days from 18% to 25%' is a measurable outcome. Workshops, hiring and redesigns are activities.

questions.q: Why must a PIP be genuine rather than a formality?
options: Fairness, trust and legal defensibility require a real chance to succeed
questions.why: A PIP must be genuine, since fairness, trust and legal defensibility require a real chance to succeed.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Motivation, psychological safety and team dynamics
courses.summary: What motivates people, how to build psychological safety, how teams develop (Tuckman), and how to handle conflict using the Thomas–Kilmann modes.
outcomes: Learners can apply Herzberg's two-factor theory and autonomy–mastery–purpose
Learners can build psychological safety with concrete behaviours
Learners can recognise Tuckman's stages and lead each
Learners can choose an appropriate conflict-handling mode

scenes.text: After a brutal quarter, a manager throws a pizza party to boost morale. Nothing changes.
In 1:1s, people mention unclear priorities and no say in decisions.

steps.title: Herzberg's two-factor theory
steps.body:
- **Hygiene factors** (salary, policies, working conditions, job security, relationships): if poor, cause dissatisfaction; fixing them removes dissatisfaction but doesn't create strong motivation.
- **Motivators** (achievement, recognition, meaningful work, responsibility, growth): create satisfaction and drive.

steps.title: Autonomy, mastery, purpose
steps.body: Daniel Pink's summary of research on motivation for complex work: **Autonomy** (control over how), **Mastery** (getting better at something that matters), **Purpose** (connection to something bigger).

steps.title: Solved example: diagnose the team
steps.body:
Complaints: unclear priorities, no say, no growth.
**Hygiene?** Partly (clarity). **Motivators missing:** autonomy and growth.
**Actions:** clear quarterly priorities; let the team choose how to deliver; rotate stretch assignments; connect work to customer impact in reviews.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using perks to fix a lack of meaning or fairness.
- Ignoring hygiene factors (e.g. pay well below market) and preaching purpose.

activity.prompt: Herzberg: hygiene factor or motivator?

items.text: Fair salary
Recognition for achievement
Clean, safe office
Responsibility for a meaningful project
Company policies
Growth and learning

quiz.why: Hygiene factors, like pay and policies, mainly prevent dissatisfaction. They don't create strong motivation.
Pink's three drivers are autonomy, mastery and purpose.
In Herzberg's model, recognition is a motivator, not a hygiene factor.
A pizza party can't fix the lack of autonomy and clarity, which are root causes of poor motivation.
Pay far below market causes dissatisfaction even when the work has purpose. This is a hygiene factor.

scenes.text: A junior engineer noticed a risky bug before release but stayed quiet — the last person who raised a concern was mocked.
The manager realises the real bug is the team's culture.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: **Psychological safety** (Amy Edmondson) is a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — people can ask questions, admit mistakes, raise concerns and offer ideas without fear of humiliation or punishment. Google's Project Aristotle research found it the most important factor among those it studied for team effectiveness.

steps.title: Behaviours that build it
steps.body:
- Frame work as learning: 'We'll hit surprises; I need your eyes.'
- Admit your own mistakes first.
- Ask questions and genuinely listen.
- Respond to bad news with thanks, not blame.
- Blameless post-mortems: focus on systems, not culprits.
- Make sure quiet voices get airtime.

steps.title: Solved example: responding to a mistake
steps.body:
Junior: 'I deleted the wrong config in staging.'
**Blaming:** 'How could you be so careless?'
**Safe:** 'Thanks for flagging fast. Let's fix it together, then look at why the tool let that happen and add a guard.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing safety with lowering standards — high safety + high standards = learning zone.
- Sarcasm in meetings.

statements.s: Psychological safety means never giving critical feedback.
statements.why: It enables candid feedback with high standards.

statements.s: Leaders admitting mistakes increases safety.
Blameless post-mortems focus on systems, not individuals.
Mocking a question has no effect on future speaking up.

quiz.q: Psychological safety concept is associated with:
quiz.why: Psychological safety is associated with Amy Edmondson.

quiz.q: Best response to someone admitting a mistake:
quiz.why: Thank someone who admits a mistake and fix the system. This encourages people to report problems.
High safety plus high standards creates the learning zone in Edmondson's framework.
Blameless post-mortems focus on systems and processes, not on finding a culprit.
Inviting quiet voices builds safety by including everyone. Sarcasm, interruption and blame damage it.

scenes.text: Five people from different teams form a new squad. Week 1: polite. Week 3: arguments about tools.
By month 3 they've found their rhythm.

steps.title: Tuckman's stages
steps.body:
Bruce Tuckman (1965; 'adjourning' added 1977):
- **Forming:** polite, unclear roles → leader gives **direction and clarity**.
- **Storming:** conflict over approach, roles → leader **coaches, mediates, sets norms**.
- **Norming:** agreed ways of working → leader **supports and delegates more**.
- **Performing:** high autonomy and output → leader **delegates, removes blockers, develops**.
- **Adjourning:** project ends → leader **recognises, captures lessons, helps transitions**.

steps.title: Solved example: identify the stage
steps.body: 'We keep arguing whether to use Jira or Trello, and two people are competing to lead.' → **Storming**. Action: facilitate a decision, agree roles and team charter.

steps.title: Teams can go back
steps.body: New members, reorganisations or crises can push a performing team back to storming. Revisit norms when the team changes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Avoiding storming conflict — it must be worked through.
- Micromanaging a performing team.

activity.prompt: Order Tuckman's stages.

quiz.q: Conflict over roles and approach typically happens in:
quiz.why: Conflict over roles and approach typically happens in the storming stage of Tuckman's model.

quiz.q: In forming, the leader should mainly:
quiz.why: In forming, the leader should provide direction and clarity, because members are still orienting.

options: Wrapping up and recognising the team
quiz.why: Adjourning is wrapping up and recognising the team at the end of its work.

options: Send the team back to an earlier stage
quiz.why: A new member joining can send the team back to an earlier stage, since dynamics change.

quiz.q: For a performing team, the leader should:
quiz.why: For a performing team, the leader should delegate and remove blockers, giving autonomy.

scenes.text: Design wants a pixel-perfect animation; engineering says it will delay launch by two weeks.
Their manager helps them find a solution both can back.

steps.title: Five modes (assertiveness × cooperativeness)
steps.body:
- **Competing** (high assert, low coop): win — use for emergencies or ethics/safety.
- **Collaborating** (high, high): find a win-win — for important issues with time.
- **Compromising** (medium, medium): split the difference — when time is short.
- **Avoiding** (low, low): sidestep — for trivial issues or to cool down.
- **Accommodating** (low assert, high coop): give way — when the issue matters more to them or to build goodwill.

steps.title: Solved example: design vs engineering
steps.body:
**Collaborate:** shared goal = great launch on time.
**Options:** ship a simpler animation at launch and the full version in the next sprint; use a library to cut effort.
**Agreement:** simple version now (launch on date), full version in 2 weeks. Both needs met.

steps.title: Conflict conversation steps
steps.body: 1) Separate people from the problem. 2) Each states interests (why), not just positions (what). 3) Agree shared goals. 4) Generate options. 5) Agree criteria and decide. 6) Write down who does what.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Always avoiding — problems grow.
- Always competing — damages trust.
- Letting conflict become personal.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the most suitable mode.
pairs: Safety violation on a site — must stop now
Deadline in an hour, two reasonable options
Trivial disagreement about a slide colour
Issue matters far more to the other person

quiz.why: High assertiveness with high cooperativeness is the collaborating conflict mode.

options: Safety or ethics is at stake
quiz.why: Use competing when safety or ethics is at stake, where a firm stance is needed. For trivial issues it damages relationships.
Focusing on interests means asking 'Why do you want that?' to uncover the underlying need.
Avoiding is appropriate for trivial issues or when people need to cool down. It's wrong for fraud, safety or recurring problems.
Compromise means each side gives something up to reach agreement.

questions.q: Herzberg's motivators include:
questions.why: Herzberg's motivators include recognition and growth. Salary and policies are hygiene factors.

questions.q: Tuckman's second stage:
questions.why: Tuckman's second stage is storming, after forming.

questions.q: Psychological safety allows people to:
questions.why: Psychological safety allows people to speak up without fear of embarrassment or punishment.

questions.q: Pink's 'mastery' means:
questions.why: In Pink's model, mastery means getting better at meaningful work.

questions.q: Conflict mode giving way to others:
questions.why: Accommodating is the conflict mode of giving way to others, with low assertiveness.

questions.q: Blameless post-mortems build:
questions.why: Blameless post-mortems build psychological safety, since people can share mistakes without fear.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Raising salaries alone will greatly increase motivation. Reason (R): Salary is a hygiene factor in Herzberg's model.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: salary is a hygiene factor in Herzberg's model, so raising it removes dissatisfaction but doesn't greatly increase motivation.

questions.q: Team argues over tools and leadership:
questions.why: A team arguing over tools and leadership is in the storming stage.

questions.q: High safety + low standards leads to:
questions.why: High safety with low standards leads to the comfort zone in Edmondson's framework.

questions.q: Collaborating requires:
options: Time and willingness to explore interests
questions.why: Collaborating requires time and willingness to explore interests, to find a win-win.

questions.q: Case: A senior keeps ridiculing juniors' questions in standup. Manager action?
options: Address privately with SBI, set team norms, model curiosity
questions.why: Address the ridicule privately using SBI, set team norms and model curiosity. Ignoring it or banning questions harms safety.

questions.q: Case: Performing team gets 3 new members and friction rises. What's happening and what to do?
options: Regression to storming; revisit norms and roles
questions.why: New members can send a performing team back into storming, so revisit norms and roles. Disbanding or micromanaging forever isn't needed.

questions.q: Case: Two leads disagree; the decision is reversible and due in 30 minutes. Best mode?
options: Compromise (or time-boxed decision by the owner)
questions.why: With a reversible decision due in 30 minutes, compromise or a time-boxed decision by the owner fits. Collaborating for weeks isn't feasible.

questions.q: Which combination best motivates knowledge workers?
options: Fair pay (hygiene) + autonomy, mastery and purpose
questions.why: Fair pay (the hygiene factor) plus autonomy, mastery and purpose motivates knowledge workers best. Control, fear or perks alone don't.

questions.q: Why does psychological safety improve performance?
options: Problems and ideas surface early so the team learns and corrects faster
questions.why: Psychological safety improves performance because problems and ideas surface early, so the team learns and corrects faster.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Workplace communication
courses.summary: Clear writing and emails, meetings that produce decisions, active listening and assertive speech, and handling difficult conversations and stakeholder updates.
outcomes: Learners can write emails with the bottom line up front
Learners can run meetings with agendas, decisions and owners
Learners can listen actively and speak assertively with I-statements
Learners can prepare difficult conversations and write RAG status updates

scenes.text: Ajay sends his VP a long email; the actual request is in paragraph five.
The VP never gets there. No decision is made.

steps.title: BLUF — bottom line up front
steps.body: Start with the **ask or conclusion**, then the reasons and details. Busy readers decide in the first two lines whether to act.

steps.title: Solved example: rewrite
steps.body:
**Subject:** Approval needed by Thu: ₹4 L for load testing
**Body:**
Hi Meera — **please approve ₹4 lakh** for a load-testing tool by Thursday so we can test before the 15 Dec sale.
Why: last sale we had a 40-minute outage; testing reduces that risk.
Options: (A) tool ₹4 L, 2 weeks; (B) manual tests, ₹0, 5 weeks (misses the sale). I recommend A.
Thanks, Ajay

steps.title: Writing habits
steps.body:
- One email = one topic; clear subject with action and date.
- Short paragraphs, bullets, bold the ask.
- Use plain words; explain acronyms.
- Re-read for tone; never write in anger — wait an hour.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Burying the request.
- Reply-all for personal replies.
- Vague subjects like 'Update' or 'Hi'.

activity.prompt: Order a BLUF email.
items: The ask or conclusion in the first line
Details or links for those who want more

quiz.why: BLUF means bottom line up front: put the conclusion or ask first.
A good subject line includes the action and deadline, so it is scannable.
When angry, wait before sending, because tone can damage relationships.
One email should cover one main topic, for clarity.

quiz.q: Offering options with a recommendation helps:
quiz.why: Offering options with a recommendation speeds up decisions, since the reader can just choose.

scenes.text: A one-hour meeting ends with 'let's sync again next week'.
Next time the organiser sends an agenda with the decision needed — it ends in 25 minutes with owners.

steps.title: Before
steps.body: Ask: does this need a meeting, or would a message/doc do? If yes: **purpose**, **desired outcome** (decision, plan, brainstorm), agenda with times, pre-read, only needed people.

steps.title: During and after
steps.body: Start on time; state the outcome; a facilitator keeps time; capture **decisions, action items (owner + date) and open questions**; send notes within 24 hours.

steps.title: Solved example: meeting notes
steps.body:
**Decisions:** Launch on 20 Jan with simple animation.
**Actions:** Rohit — update release plan by Fri; Meera — inform client by Mon.
**Open:** Full animation scope → design review Wed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No agenda; no decision owner.
- 15 people invited 'for visibility'.
- Ending without action items.

activity.prompt: Meeting checklist
items: Purpose and desired outcome stated in the invite
Decisions and actions with owners and dates captured

quiz.why: Every meeting should have a clear purpose and outcome, which keeps it focused.
Action items need an owner and a date, for accountability.

options: Could a message or doc do?
quiz.why: Before scheduling a meeting, ask whether a message or doc could do the job. This avoids wasted time.
Send meeting notes within 24 hours to keep momentum.
Inviting many people 'for visibility' wastes time; share notes instead.

scenes.text: Shalini keeps getting extra work dumped on her. She either says yes or explodes.
She learns a third way: assertive communication.

steps.title: Active listening
steps.body:
- Give full attention (no phone).
- **Paraphrase:** 'So what I'm hearing is…'
- **Ask open questions:** 'What would help most?'
- **Reflect feelings:** 'That sounds frustrating.'
- **Summarise** and confirm next steps.

steps.title: Passive, aggressive, assertive
steps.body:
- **Passive:** own needs ignored ('It's fine…').
- **Aggressive:** others' needs ignored ('You always dump work on me!').
- **Passive-aggressive:** indirect hostility (sarcasm, silent treatment).
- **Assertive:** respects both: clear, calm, honest.

steps.title: Solved example: I-statement
steps.body:
Formula: **When** [specific event], **I feel** [feeling], **because** [impact]. **I'd like** [request].
'When new tasks arrive at 6 pm on Fridays, I feel stressed because I can't plan my weekend. I'd like us to agree new tasks by Thursday noon unless it's urgent.'

steps.title: Saying no well
steps.body: 'I can't take this on and still deliver X by Friday. Which should I prioritise?' — puts the trade-off on the table.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listening only to reply.
- 'You always/never' statements.
- Apologising excessively for reasonable requests.

activity.prompt: Passive, aggressive or assertive?

items.text: 'Sure, no problem' (while already overloaded)
'You're useless at planning!'
'I can do this if we move the report to Monday — okay?'
'Whatever you say…' (sighing)
'When I'm interrupted, I lose my point. Could I finish first?'

quiz.why: Paraphrasing shows you understood what was said, as part of active listening.
Assertive communication respects both your needs and others'.
I-statements follow the form 'When…, I feel…', describing the effect on you without blame.
Saying no well includes stating the trade-off, so priorities are clear. Ignoring or saying yes and missing it is worse.
Sarcasm and the silent treatment are passive-aggressive, a form of indirect hostility.

scenes.text: A project is two weeks behind. The PM keeps reporting 'green' hoping to catch up.
At launch week it becomes red — and trust collapses.

steps.title: Preparing a difficult conversation
steps.body: 1) Clarify your goal and the facts. 2) Consider their perspective and interests. 3) Open with purpose: 'I'd like to talk about X because I want Y.' 4) Share facts and impact (SBI). 5) Listen. 6) Problem-solve together. 7) Agree next steps in writing.

steps.title: RAG status
steps.body:
- **Green:** on track.
- **Amber:** at risk; recovery plan in place; may need help.
- **Red:** off track; decisions or help needed now.
Good updates: status, what changed, risks/issues, decisions needed, next steps — bad news **early**, with options.

steps.title: Solved example: an honest amber update
steps.body:
**Status: Amber.** API integration is 1 week behind because the vendor's sandbox was down for 4 days.
**Impact:** launch at risk by up to 1 week.
**Options:** (A) add 1 contractor, ₹1.5 L, keeps date; (B) move launch 1 week.
**Decision needed by Wed:** A or B. Recommendation: A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Watermelon' status: green outside, red inside.
- Delivering bad news without options.
- Having hard conversations over chat when a call would be kinder.

a.text: Your project slipped 10 days. The steering meeting is tomorrow. What status do you report?

choices.label: Green — we might catch up
Amber with the cause, impact, options and a decision needed

b.text: Two weeks later it's obviously late. Leadership asks why they weren't told. What now?

choices.label: Own it, give the real status and options, and commit to honest updates

c.text: Leadership picks option A (add a contractor). What's your follow-up?

choices.label: Send written notes with decision, owners and dates

d.text: The project lands 2 days late instead of 10, and leadership trusts your updates. Bad news early is good management.

options: At risk, with a recovery plan
quiz.why: Amber means at risk, with a recovery plan. Green is on track and red is off track.
Watermelon status is green on the outside and red inside, hiding real problems.
Share bad news early with options, so there is time to act.
Open a difficult conversation with the purpose and the shared goal. Threats or accusations create defensiveness.
Good status updates include the decisions needed, so they are actionable.

questions.q: BLUF puts first:
questions.why: BLUF puts the ask or conclusion first, before the background.

questions.q: Red status means:
questions.why: Red status means off track, with help or decisions needed.

questions.q: Assertive statement:
options: 'I'd like to finish my point, please.'
questions.why: 'I'd like to finish my point, please' is assertive and respectful. 'Shut up' is aggressive and silence or 'fine, whatever' is passive.

questions.q: Meeting notes must capture:
questions.why: Meeting notes must capture decisions and actions with owners. Jokes or latecomers add nothing.

questions.q: Paraphrasing is part of:
questions.why: Paraphrasing is part of active listening.

questions.q: A good email subject:
questions.why: 'Decision needed by Fri: vendor choice' states the action and date. 'Update', 'Hi' or blank subjects don't.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Reporting green while behind protects the team. Reason (R): Early warnings give leaders time to help.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: reporting green while behind hides the problem, whereas early warnings give leaders time to help.

questions.q: 'When deadlines change late, I feel stressed because… I'd like…' is a:
questions.why: 'When deadlines change late, I feel stressed because… I'd like…' follows the I-statement formula.

questions.q: Before scheduling a meeting, first ask:
questions.why: Before scheduling a meeting, first ask whether async communication could work.

questions.q: Difficult conversations should usually be:
questions.why: Difficult conversations should usually be live, by call or in person, rather than by chat, because tone and nuance matter.

questions.q: Case: Your manager asks you to take a big new task; you're at capacity. Best reply?
options: 'I can, if we move X to next week — which matters more?'
questions.why: 'I can, if we move X to next week — which matters more?' states the trade-off clearly. A silent yes that misses deadlines or a flat no doesn't help.

questions.q: Case: VP doesn't respond to your long email. Best fix?
options: Resend with the ask and deadline in the first line and options
questions.why: Resend with the ask and deadline in the first line and options (BLUF), because a long email buries the point. Copying everyone or resending unchanged doesn't help.

questions.q: Case: In a 1-hour meeting, no decision is reached and people talk past each other. Best facilitation move?
options: Restate the decision needed, list options and criteria, ask the owner to decide
questions.why: Restate the decision needed, list options and criteria, and ask the owner to decide. This gives the meeting structure.

questions.q: Which update is best?
options: 'Amber: test env delay 4 days; impact 1 week; options A/B; decision needed Wed'
questions.why: The best update is complete and actionable: the status, cause, impact, options and the decision needed. 'All good' or 'some issues' tells nothing.

questions.q: Why does assertive communication improve working relationships?
options: It's clear and respectful, so problems are solved without resentment
questions.why: Assertive communication is clear and respectful, so problems are solved without resentment. It doesn't always win or avoid conflict.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Decisions, leadership styles and leading change
courses.summary: Situational leadership, decision rights with RACI, decision-making under uncertainty, and leading change with Kotter's eight steps.
outcomes: Learners can adapt leadership style to development level
Learners can build a RACI and avoid unclear ownership
Learners can make reversible decisions fast and irreversible ones carefully, using pre-mortems
Learners can plan a change using Kotter's steps

scenes.text: Manager Faisal gives everyone full freedom. His senior engineers thrive; two new graduates are lost.
He learns to adjust style to each person and task.

steps.title: The model
steps.body:
The **Situational Leadership** model (Hersey and Blanchard) matches style to the follower's competence and commitment **for a specific task**:
- **Directing/Telling** (high direction, low support): new, enthusiastic but inexperienced.
- **Coaching/Selling** (high direction, high support): some skill, low confidence/commitment.
- **Supporting/Participating** (low direction, high support): capable but hesitant.
- **Delegating** (low, low): capable and committed.

steps.title: Solved example: match styles
steps.body:
- Graduate on first deployment → **Directing**: step-by-step checklist, close check-ins.
- Mid-level dev frustrated after failed attempts → **Coaching**: explain why, encourage, guide.
- Senior who doubts readiness to lead a design review → **Supporting**: ask their view, boost confidence.
- Senior expert on routine release → **Delegating**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- One style for everyone.
- Labelling a person permanently — development level is per task.
- Delegating to someone who lacks skill ('sink or swim').

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the leadership style.
pairs: New hire, eager, no experience on this task
Expert and motivated on routine work

quiz.why: Situational leadership was developed by Hersey and Blanchard.
High direction with low support is the directing style, suited to beginners.
Development level is assessed per task, not by age or once for life, because someone can be expert in one task and new in another.
For capable and committed people, delegating fits, as they can work autonomously.
'Sink or swim' for beginners is a mismatched style, because beginners need direction.

scenes.text: A pricing change goes live. Sales says they weren't consulted; Finance says they never approved.
A RACI chart would have prevented the confusion.

steps.title: RACI
steps.body:
- **Responsible:** does the work (can be several).
- **Accountable:** owns the outcome and final decision (**exactly one** per task).
- **Consulted:** gives input before (two-way).
- **Informed:** told after (one-way).

steps.title: Solved example: pricing change
steps.body:
| Task: change plan prices |
- Pricing analyst — **R**
- Head of Product — **A**
- Finance, Sales — **C**
- Support, Marketing — **I**
Result: one accountable owner, input collected first, others told before go-live.

steps.title: Other tools
steps.body: For decisions, some teams use **DACI** (Driver, Approver, Contributors, Informed). Whatever the tool, name one decision owner and the decision date.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Two 'A's — nobody really owns it.
- Everyone 'C' — decisions stall.
- RACI made once and never shared.

activity.prompt: RACI for 'launch a new onboarding email'.

items.text: Copywriter drafting the email
Growth lead who approves and owns results
Legal reviewing the wording
Support team told the launch date

quiz.why: In RACI there should be exactly one Accountable person per task, so ownership is clear.
Consulted means giving input before the decision, a two-way exchange. Being told afterwards is Informed.
Informed means the person is told after a decision, which is one-way communication. Consulted gives input before.
Too many people in the 'Consulted' role causes stalled decisions, because of the overhead of gathering every view.
In RACI, 'R' (Responsible) is the person who does the work. The approver is Accountable.

scenes.text: A team spends six weeks analysing which colour button converts better.
Their director says: 'It's a two-way door. Test it this week.'

steps.title: One-way vs two-way doors
steps.body: **Reversible** decisions (two-way doors): decide fast with ~70% of the information, test and adjust. **Irreversible or costly-to-reverse** decisions (one-way doors: big hires, acquisitions, architecture choices, layoffs): slow down, gather input, consider options carefully.

steps.title: Pre-mortem
steps.body: Before committing, imagine it's a year later and the decision **failed**. Each person writes why. This surfaces risks people hesitate to raise. Then add mitigations.

steps.title: Solved example: classify and act
steps.body:
- Change onboarding email subject → two-way; A/B test this week.
- Migrate the whole platform to a new database → one-way-ish; pre-mortem, proof of concept, staged rollout, rollback plan.
- Hire a VP → one-way; structured interviews, references, panel.

steps.title: Decision hygiene
steps.body: Write the decision, options, criteria and expected outcome; review later to learn (decision journal). Separate decision quality from outcome luck.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating every decision as one-way (slow) or as two-way (reckless).
- Groupthink — invite dissent; ask someone to argue the opposite.

activity.prompt: Two-way door (decide fast) or one-way door (decide carefully)?

items.text: Try a new meeting format for a month
Sign a 5-year exclusive vendor contract
Change a landing-page headline
Close an office
Pilot a new tool with one team
Acquire a startup

quiz.q: Two-way door decisions should be made:
quiz.why: Two-way door decisions are reversible, so make them quickly and adjust later. Slow analysis costs more than a small mistake.

options: The project has failed and asks why
quiz.why: A pre-mortem imagines the project has already failed and asks why. This surfaces risks before you commit.

options: Separately from luck in the outcome
quiz.why: Decision quality should be judged separately from luck in the outcome. A good decision can still turn out badly.
Groupthink is reduced by inviting dissent, which brings diverse views. Silencing critics increases it.
Acquisitions are usually one-way doors, as they are hard to undo, so they deserve more care.

scenes.text: IT rolls out a new project tool by email. Six months later, teams still use spreadsheets.
A second attempt follows a change model — and sticks.

steps.title: Kotter's eight steps
steps.body:
John Kotter's model (1996):
1) Create a sense of **urgency**
2) Build a **guiding coalition**
3) Form a strategic **vision**
4) **Communicate** the vision (enlist a volunteer army)
5) **Remove barriers** (enable action)
6) Generate **short-term wins**
7) **Sustain** acceleration
8) **Anchor** changes in culture

steps.title: Solved example: tool rollout, done right
steps.body: 1) Show data: 30% of deadlines missed due to scattered tracking. 2) Champions from each team. 3) Vision: 'One place to see all work.' 4) Demos, FAQs, leaders using it visibly. 5) Migrate templates, train, remove old spreadsheets' approvals. 6) Celebrate first team that hits all deadlines. 7) Expand to all teams. 8) Make it part of onboarding and reviews.

steps.title: People in change
steps.body: People move through reactions like shock, resistance, exploration and commitment at different speeds. Listen to concerns — resistance often contains useful information.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Announcing change by email only.
- Declaring victory too early.
- Ignoring the 'what's in it for me?' question.

activity.prompt: Order Kotter's eight steps.

quiz.why: Kotter's first step is to create urgency, so people feel the need to change.
Short-term wins build momentum and credibility by proving the change works.

options: Embedding it in culture and processes
quiz.why: Anchoring change means embedding it in culture and processes so it lasts.
Resistance to change often contains useful information, so listen to it. It isn't always irrational or a reason to fire people.
Declaring victory too early risks the change sliding back, as Kotter warns, because it isn't yet anchored.

questions.q: RACI 'A' means:
questions.why: In RACI, A stands for Accountable, the single owner of the result.

questions.q: Kotter's step 1:
questions.why: Kotter's step 1 is to create urgency.

questions.q: Delegating style suits:
questions.why: A delegating style suits capable, committed people, who need little direction or support.

questions.q: Two-way door decisions are:
questions.why: Two-way door decisions are reversible, so you can walk back through if it goes wrong.

questions.q: Number of 'A' per task:
questions.why: Each task should have exactly one 'A' (Accountable) for clear ownership.

questions.q: A pre-mortem helps to:
questions.why: A pre-mortem helps to surface risks before committing, by imagining failure in advance.

questions.q: Assertion (A): One leadership style fits all team members. Reason (R): Development level varies by person and task.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: development level varies by person and task, so situational leadership says one style doesn't fit all.

questions.q: Coaching style =
questions.why: The coaching style is high direction and high support, for people who are keen but still learning.

questions.q: Kotter step after 'communicate the vision':
questions.why: In Kotter's model, after communicating the vision you remove barriers, so people can act on it.

questions.q: Consulted vs Informed:
options: Consulted gives input before; Informed told after
questions.why: Consulted gives input before the decision, while Informed is told afterwards.

questions.q: Case: Two directors both think they approve a launch. Fix?
questions.why: A RACI with one Accountable owner resolves who approves, so two directors don't both think they decide.

questions.q: Case: Team debates a reversible UI change for 6 weeks. Advice?
options: Treat as two-way door: test quickly and iterate
questions.why: A reversible UI change is a two-way door, so test quickly and iterate instead of debating for weeks.

questions.q: Case: A capable senior lacks confidence to present to the board. Style?
questions.why: A capable person lacking confidence needs low direction but high support, which is the supporting style.

questions.q: Case: A new process was adopted for 2 months, then teams slid back. Which Kotter steps were likely skipped?
options: Sustain acceleration and anchor in culture
questions.why: If teams slid back after 2 months, the later steps were likely skipped: sustaining acceleration and anchoring the change in culture.

questions.q: Why separate decision quality from outcome?
options: Good decisions can have bad luck; judging only outcomes teaches wrong lessons
questions.why: Separate decision quality from outcome, because a good decision can have bad luck. Judging only outcomes teaches the wrong lessons.

courses.title: Management · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: A one-page model sheet, a scenario drill applying the right model, and a full mock test.
outcomes: Learners can recall every model in the course
Learners can pick the right model for a situation
Learners can score 80%+ on the mock

scenes.text: Kavya keeps a pocket card of models for quick reference.
Before every tough conversation she checks it.

steps.title: People models
steps.body:
- Delegation levels 1–5 · Eisenhower matrix
- SBI feedback · GROW coaching
- SMART goals · OKRs (objective + 2–5 measurable KRs)
- Herzberg (hygiene vs motivators) · Pink (autonomy, mastery, purpose)
- Psychological safety (Edmondson)
- Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning
- Thomas–Kilmann: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating

steps.title: Communication & decisions
steps.body:
- BLUF emails · meetings with outcome, decisions, owners
- Active listening · I-statements · assertiveness
- RAG status, bad news early with options
- Situational leadership: directing, coaching, supporting, delegating
- RACI (one A) · two-way vs one-way doors · pre-mortem
- Kotter's 8 steps

steps.title: Top mistakes
steps.body: Super-IC bottleneck · vague feedback · surprise ratings · tasks as KRs · perks instead of meaning · watermelon status · two Accountables · email-only change

quiz.why: Recognition is a Herzberg motivator. Salary, office and policies are hygiene factors.
Key Results should be measurable outcomes, not tasks or vague statements.
Collaborating is the win-win conflict mode in Thomas–Kilmann, with high assertiveness and high cooperativeness.
For experts, delegating is the best situational style, giving autonomy.

scenes.text: Six real situations, one minute each.
Name the model and the first move.

steps.title: 1) Vague annual goal
steps.body: 'Improve quality' → **SMART** → 'Reduce escaped defects from 12 to 4 per release by Q3.'

steps.title: 2) Junior brings every problem
steps.body: → **GROW** coaching questions to build ownership.

steps.title: 3) Peer interrupts others
steps.body: → **SBI** feedback in private.

steps.title: 4) New squad arguing
steps.body: → **Tuckman storming** → facilitate norms and roles.

steps.title: 5) Confusion over who approves
steps.body: → **RACI** with one Accountable.

steps.title: 6) Rolling out a new process
steps.body: → **Kotter** — start with urgency and a coalition.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the model.
pairs: Need to give specific corrective feedback
Deciding whether to analyse or just test

quiz.why: For a vague goal, use SMART to make it specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
RACI clarifies who approves and who does what, so it handles decision rights.
Kotter's model guides big organisational change.
SBI (Situation, Behaviour, Impact) is the model for corrective feedback.

scenes.text: Take the mock in 25 minutes.
Revisit chapters where you miss two or more.

steps.title: Case-question method
steps.body: 1) Name the problem type (goal, feedback, motivation, conflict, decision, change). 2) Pick the model. 3) Choose the answer that is **specific, fair, early and two-way**.

steps.title: Practise for real
steps.body: This week: one SBI feedback, one GROW conversation, one BLUF email, and one RACI for a live task.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Models are tools, not scripts. Adapt to people and context, and stay kind and honest.

activity.prompt: Which model will you use this week, with whom, and for what?
activity.hint: e.g. 'SBI with Aman about late updates on Wednesday.'

quiz.why: Good case answers are specific, fair, early and two-way. Harsh, avoidant or vague late responses cause harm.
Models are tools to adapt to the situation, not rigid scripts or laws.
The first step on a case is to name the problem type, since diagnosing it tells you which model fits.

questions.q: BLUF:
questions.why: BLUF means bottom line up front.

questions.q: SMART 'R':
questions.why: In SMART, R stands for Relevant.

questions.q: GROW 'W':
questions.why: In GROW, W stands for Will, or the way forward: what you will do.

questions.q: Tuckman stage after norming:
questions.why: After norming comes performing in Tuckman's model.

questions.q: Hygiene factor:
questions.why: Salary is a hygiene factor in Herzberg's model. Growth, achievement and recognition are motivators.

questions.q: Collaborating is:
questions.why: Collaborating has high assertiveness and high cooperativeness.

questions.q: Eisenhower 'important not urgent':
questions.why: In the Eisenhower matrix, important but not urgent tasks are scheduled.

questions.q: Amber status:
questions.why: Amber status means at risk, with a plan to recover.

questions.q: KR from 40% to 60%; achieved 55%. Score?
questions.why: Score = progress ÷ target change = (55 − 40) ÷ (60 − 40) = 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Psychological safety lowers standards. Reason (R): Safe teams can discuss mistakes openly.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: safe teams can discuss mistakes openly, so psychological safety doesn't lower standards; high safety with high standards gives the learning zone.

questions.q: Calibration question to reduce bias:
questions.why: 'What's the evidence?' reduces bias in calibration by pushing the discussion towards facts.

questions.q: One Accountable per task in RACI because:
questions.why: One Accountable per task gives clear ownership, which prevents confusion about who decides.

questions.q: Case: Engineer delivers late after being moved to an unfamiliar domain with no training. First move?
questions.why: If an engineer is late after moving to an unfamiliar domain with no training, diagnose and provide training or pairing. A PIP or public warning ignores the skill gap.

questions.q: Case: Team survey shows people fear raising concerns. Best first move by manager?
options: Admit own mistakes, thank bad-news bearers, run blameless reviews
questions.why: Build safety by admitting your own mistakes, thanking bad-news bearers and running blameless reviews. Telling people to be brave or punishing complaints makes it worse.

questions.q: Case: A safety issue on a factory floor; a supervisor wants to discuss options for a week. Conflict mode?
questions.why: With a safety issue on the factory floor, a competing mode, stopping the line now, is right. Safety shouldn't wait a week for compromise.

questions.q: Case: Rolling out hybrid-work policy; staff anxious. Kotter-aligned first steps?
options: Explain urgency with data, form a coalition, share a clear vision and FAQs
questions.why: Kotter's early steps are to explain urgency with data, form a coalition and share a clear vision and FAQs. Silent mandates cause anxiety.

questions.q: Which is the BEST SBI?
options: 'In Monday's client call, you shared the wrong pricing sheet; the client got confused and asked for a re-quote.'
questions.why: The best SBI names the situation (Monday's client call), the behaviour (wrong pricing sheet) and the impact (client confusion and re-quote). The others are labels or hearsay.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Directing → new and inexperienced; Delegating → capable and committed
questions.why: Directing suits new and inexperienced people, while delegating suits capable and committed ones. The other pairings are mismatched.

questions.q: Why are stretch OKRs not tied directly to individual bonuses?
options: To avoid sandbagging and encourage ambitious goals
questions.why: Stretch OKRs aren't tied directly to bonuses to avoid sandbagging, so teams stay ambitious.

questions.q: Which update shows the best communication?
options: 'Amber: vendor delay 5 days; impact 1 week; options A/B; decision needed Wed; recommend A'
questions.why: The best update is honest and actionable: amber status, the delay, the impact, the options, the decision needed and a recommendation. 'Green' while behind or 'some issues' tells nothing.

corp-politics-2.title: Office politics in Indian workplaces: real scenarios, part 2
corp-politics-2.description: A deeper, scenario-driven course on navigating power, managers, peers, appraisals, boundaries and exits in Indian offices — ethically, without losing yourself. Every lesson has a branching scenario.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Mapping power and building influence
courses.summary: Formal vs informal power, stakeholder mapping, the difference between mentors and sponsors, and building genuine allies — the ethical foundations of influence.
outcomes: Learners can tell formal authority from informal influence
Learners can draw a power–interest stakeholder map
Learners can explain mentors vs sponsors and how to earn sponsorship
Learners can build a network through reciprocity, not flattery

scenes.text: Fresher Aakash pitches his idea to the Director and gets a polite nod. Nothing happens.
A senior tells him: 'Before anything reaches the Director, Sunita ma'am from Finance looks at it. Talk to her first.'
Aakash learns that the org chart shows authority, not always influence.

steps.title: Two kinds of power
steps.body:
- **Formal (positional) power:** comes from title and reporting lines — approving budgets, ratings, hiring.
- **Informal power:** comes from expertise, relationships, information, reputation and tenure — the long-time architect everyone consults, the EA who manages the VP's calendar, the finance controller who vets every proposal.

steps.title: Sources of influence
steps.body: Expertise · trusted relationships · access to information · track record of delivering · being helpful and generous · controlling scarce resources (budget, headcount, servers). In many Indian offices, **tenure and relationships** carry a lot of weight.

steps.title: Solved example: who to talk to
steps.body:
Aakash wants a new testing tool.
**Formal:** Director approves budget.
