courses.title: Ch 2 · Scaling services and load balancing
courses.summary: Vertical vs horizontal scaling, stateless services and sessions, load balancers and algorithms, health checks, autoscaling, and why consistent hashing exists.
outcomes: Learners can choose between vertical and horizontal scaling
Learners can make services stateless
Learners can compare load-balancing algorithms and L4 vs L7
Learners can explain consistent hashing and why modulo hashing reshuffles keys

story.title: The biggest server we could buy

scenes.text: A ticketing startup keeps upgrading to bigger machines before every concert sale.
At the largest size, one crash takes the whole site down.
They redesign to many small, stateless servers.

steps.title: Vertical scaling (scale up)
steps.body: Bigger machine: more CPU, RAM, faster disk. **Pros:** simple, no code change. **Cons:** hardware ceiling, cost rises steeply, single point of failure, downtime to resize.

steps.title: Horizontal scaling (scale out)
steps.body: More machines behind a load balancer. **Pros:** near-linear capacity, fault tolerance, autoscaling. **Cons:** requires **stateless** design, distributed-systems complexity (consistency, coordination).

steps.title: Making services stateless
steps.body: Don't keep user session data in server memory. Store sessions in a shared store (Redis), use signed tokens (JWT) carried by clients, put files in object storage. Then **any** server can handle **any** request.

steps.title: Solved example: sticky sessions problem
steps.body:
**Setup:** sessions in server memory + load balancer with sticky sessions.
**Failure:** server 3 dies → its users are logged out and lose carts.
**Fix:** move sessions to Redis (replicated) → servers become interchangeable; sticky sessions no longer needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Scaling the app tier while the single database becomes the bottleneck.
- Writing uploads to local disk on app servers.
- Assuming horizontal scaling is always cheaper — start simple, scale when data says so.

activity.prompt: Vertical or horizontal?

items.text: Upgrade from 16 GB to 128 GB RAM
Add 10 more app servers behind a load balancer
Autoscale container replicas from 3 to 30
Move to a CPU with more cores on the same box
Add read replicas to spread reads

quiz.q: Main prerequisite for horizontal scaling of app servers:
quiz.why: Horizontal scaling needs stateless services, so any server can handle any request. Sticky sessions tie users to specific servers.

options: Hardware ceiling and single point of failure
quiz.why: Vertical scaling has a hardware ceiling and leaves a single point of failure, since you rely on one big machine.

quiz.q: Where should sessions live for stateless apps?
options: Shared store like Redis or signed tokens
quiz.why: For stateless apps, keep sessions in a shared store like Redis or in signed tokens. Local files or server RAM tie them to one server.
Uploaded files should go to object storage, which is shared and durable. App server local disks are lost or unavailable to other servers.
Horizontal scaling improves both capacity and fault tolerance, since more machines handle more load and one failure matters less.

scenes.text: With round-robin, one server handling slow video uploads is at 100% CPU while others idle.
Switching to least-connections spreads the load better.

steps.title: L4 vs L7
steps.body:
- **Layer 4 (transport):** routes by IP/port (TCP/UDP); very fast; can't see URLs or headers.
- **Layer 7 (application):** understands HTTP — route by path (`/api` vs `/images`), headers, cookies; can terminate TLS, rewrite, rate-limit.

steps.title: Algorithms
steps.body:
- **Round robin:** next server in turn — simple, assumes equal requests.
- **Weighted round robin:** bigger servers get more.
- **Least connections:** to the server with fewest active connections — good for uneven request durations.
- **IP/consistent hash:** same client/key → same server (affinity, caches).
- **Random with two choices:** pick two at random, send to the less loaded — simple and effective.

steps.title: Health checks
steps.body: The load balancer probes each server (e.g. `GET /health` every 10 s). Failing servers are removed until healthy. Use **readiness** (can take traffic?) vs **liveness** (is it alive?) checks in container platforms.

steps.title: Solved example: round robin by hand
steps.body:
Servers A, B, C; 7 requests → A, B, C, A, B, C, A.
**Request k** (0-based) goes to server `k mod 3`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A single load balancer as a new single point of failure — run it redundantly (managed LBs do this).
- Health checks that only test 'process alive' while the DB connection is broken.

activity.prompt: Round-robin: line 1 has server names separated by spaces; line 2 has N (number of requests). Print the server chosen for each request, space-separated.
activity.starter:
servers = input().split()
n = int(input())
# choose server for each request k = 0..n-1
activity.solution:
servers = input().split()
n = int(input())
print(' '.join(servers[k % len(servers)] for k in range(n)))

quiz.q: Routing /images and /api to different pools requires:
quiz.why: Routing /images and /api to different pools needs a Layer 7 load balancer, because it understands HTTP paths. Layer 4 sees only IPs and ports.

quiz.q: Best algorithm when requests vary greatly in duration:
quiz.why: When request durations vary greatly, least connections works best because it accounts for the active load on each server.
Health checks let the load balancer remove unhealthy servers from rotation, avoiding failing nodes.

quiz.q: Request number 7 (0-based) with 3 servers in round robin goes to server index:
quiz.why: Round robin with 3 servers sends request number n to index n mod 3. 7 mod 3 = 1.
A single load balancer instance is a single point of failure, so make it redundant.

scenes.text: A team uses `server = hash(key) % 4` for four cache servers.
They add a fifth server. Suddenly almost every key maps somewhere new — the cache empties and the database is flooded.

steps.title: The modulo problem
steps.body: With `hash(key) % N`, changing N changes the mapping for **most** keys. Going from N to N+1 moves roughly **N/(N+1)** of keys — e.g. ~80% when going 4 → 5.

steps.title: The ring
steps.body: **Consistent hashing** places both servers and keys on a hash ring (0 … 2³²−1). Each key belongs to the **next server clockwise**. Adding a server only takes keys from its clockwise neighbour → only about **1/N** of keys move.

steps.title: Virtual nodes
steps.body: Each physical server is placed at many points (e.g. 100–200 virtual nodes) to spread load evenly and to share the load of a failed server among many others. Used in distributed caches and databases (e.g. Dynamo-style stores, Cassandra).

steps.title: Solved example: count moved keys with modulo
steps.body: Keys 1…20, N goes 4 → 5. A key stays only if k mod 4 = k mod 5, i.e. k mod 20 ∈ {0,1,2,3} → keys 1, 2, 3, 20 → 4 stay, **16 of 20 (80%) move**. With consistent hashing, about 1/5 (20%) would move.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using modulo hashing for caches that scale up and down.
- Too few virtual nodes → uneven 'hot' servers.

activity.prompt: Read n. For keys 1..n, count how many map to a different shard when the shard count changes from 4 to 5 using key % shards. Print the count.
activity.starter:
n = int(input())
moved = 0
# loop over keys 1..n
print(moved)
activity.solution:
n = int(input())
moved = sum(1 for k in range(1, n + 1) if k % 4 != k % 5)
print(moved)

quiz.q: Going from N to N+1 servers with modulo hashing moves about:
quiz.why: With modulo hashing, going from N to N+1 servers remaps about N/(N+1) of keys, since most keys change their bucket.

quiz.q: With consistent hashing, adding a server moves about:
quiz.why: With consistent hashing, adding a server moves only about 1/N of keys, the share the new node takes from its neighbour.
Virtual nodes give each server many points on the ring, which gives an even load distribution.

quiz.q: In a hash ring, a key goes to:
quiz.why: On a hash ring, a key goes to the next server clockwise from its hash position, the successor.

quiz.q: Why does modulo remapping hurt caches?
options: Mass cache misses flood the database
quiz.why: Modulo remapping hurts caches because most keys move, causing mass cache misses that flood the database.

scenes.text: A streaming platform expects 5× traffic for a cricket final.
Autoscaling helps — but only if planned: warm capacity, limits and dependencies.

steps.title: Autoscaling basics
steps.body: Add/remove instances based on metrics: CPU, request rate per instance, queue depth, latency. Set **min/max** limits, **cooldowns** to avoid flapping, and scale on a metric that tracks user load.

steps.title: Predictable spikes
steps.body: For known events (sales, matches, results day), **pre-scale** (scheduled scaling) because new instances take minutes to boot and warm caches. Load-test beforehand.

steps.title: Solved example: how many instances?
steps.body:
Peak 50,000 RPS; each instance handles 400 RPS at target 60% CPU.
**Step 1:** 50,000 / 400 = 125 instances.
**Step 2:** +25% headroom for failures/AZ loss → ~157.
**Step 3:** Check dependencies (DB connections, third-party API limits) can handle it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Autoscaling the app while the DB connection pool caps throughput.
- Scaling on CPU for I/O-bound services.
- No max limit → runaway cost during an attack.

activity.prompt: Peak 24,000 RPS, each instance handles 300 RPS. Instances needed before headroom?

quiz.q: Why pre-scale for a known event?
options: New instances take time to boot and warm
quiz.why: Pre-scale for a known event because new instances take time to boot and warm up, so reactive autoscaling lags.
Cooldowns prevent flapping, rapid scaling up and down.

quiz.q: Good scaling metric for a queue worker:
quiz.why: Queue depth is a good scaling metric for a queue worker, since it tracks the backlog.

quiz.q: A max instance limit protects against:
quiz.why: A maximum instance limit protects against runaway cost.
Database connections are a hidden bottleneck when scaling apps, because all instances share a limited pool.

questions.q: Scale out means:
questions.why: Scale out means adding more machines, which is horizontal scaling.

questions.q: L7 load balancers can route by:
questions.why: L7 load balancers understand HTTP, so they can route by URL path.

questions.q: Stateless services store sessions:
questions.why: Stateless services store sessions externally, in Redis or tokens, so any server can serve any request.

questions.q: Round robin with 4 servers: request 10 (0-based) goes to index:
questions.why: Round robin with 4 servers sends request n to n mod 4. 10 mod 4 = 2.

questions.q: Health checks remove:
questions.why: Health checks remove unhealthy servers from routing, keeping requests safe.

questions.q: Consistent hashing primarily reduces:
questions.why: Consistent hashing primarily reduces key movement when nodes are added or removed.

questions.q: Keys 1..40, shards 4→5 with modulo: how many move?
questions.why: With modulo, a key stays only if k mod 4 equals k mod 5, which happens when k mod 20 is 0–3. In keys 1–40, those are 1, 2, 3, 20, 21, 22, 23 and 40, so 8 stay and 32 move.

questions.q: Least connections suits:
questions.why: Least connections suits variable request durations, as it sends work to the least busy server.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Sticky sessions hide statefulness problems. Reason (R): When a sticky server dies, its users lose session state.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: sticky sessions hide statefulness problems, since if the sticky server dies its users lose session state.

questions.q: Virtual nodes primarily:
options: Even out load on a hash ring
questions.why: Virtual nodes primarily even out load on a hash ring.

questions.q: Case: 60,000 RPS peak, 500 RPS per instance, 20% headroom. Instances?
questions.why: 60,000 ÷ 500 = 120 instances, and 20% headroom makes 120 × 1.2 = 144.

questions.q: Case: App autoscaled to 200 instances but throughput flat; DB shows max connections. Best fix?
options: Connection pooling/proxy and read replicas or caching
questions.why: If throughput is flat while the DB shows maximum connections, the DB is the bottleneck. Use connection pooling or a proxy, plus read replicas or caching; adding more app instances worsens it.

questions.q: Case: Video upload requests take 30 s while API calls take 50 ms on the same pool. Best design?
options: Separate pools via L7 routing and use least-connections
questions.why: Separate the slow uploads from fast API calls with L7 routing into different pools, and use least connections. Mixing them on one round-robin pool lets slow requests starve fast ones.

questions.q: Fraction of keys moved going from 9 to 10 nodes with modulo ≈
questions.why: With modulo hashing, going from 9 to 10 nodes moves N/(N+1) = 9/10 = 90% of keys.

questions.q: Why is 'power of two random choices' effective?
options: Picking the less loaded of two random servers greatly reduces max load with little coordination
questions.why: Picking the less loaded of two random servers greatly reduces the maximum load with little coordination. It is a known load-balancing result.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Caching and CDNs
courses.summary: Where to cache, cache patterns, eviction policies with an LRU implementation, invalidation and stampedes, and content delivery networks.
outcomes: Learners can choose cache-aside, read-through, write-through or write-back
Learners can implement LRU eviction
Learners can prevent stale data and cache stampedes
Learners can explain how CDNs reduce latency and load

scenes.text: An e-commerce product page makes 12 database queries; at sale time the DB melts.
Adding a Redis cache cuts DB load by 90%.

steps.title: Cache layers
steps.body: Browser cache → CDN/edge → API gateway/reverse proxy → application in-memory cache → distributed cache (Redis/Memcached) → database buffer cache. Cache as close to the user as correctness allows.

steps.title: Patterns
steps.body:
- **Cache-aside (lazy):** app checks cache; on miss reads DB and fills cache. Most common.
- **Read-through:** cache library loads from DB on miss.
- **Write-through:** write to cache and DB together — cache always fresh, writes slower.
- **Write-back (write-behind):** write to cache, flush to DB later — fast writes, risk of loss if cache fails.
- **Write-around:** write to DB only; cache filled on read.

steps.title: Solved example: hit ratio maths
steps.body:
DB read = 10 ms, cache read = 1 ms, hit ratio 90%.
**Average** = 0.9 × 1 + 0.1 × (1 + 10) = 0.9 + 1.1 = **2.0 ms** (miss pays cache check + DB).
DB load drops to 10% of reads.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Caching without a TTL — stale forever.
- Caching per-user sensitive data in a shared CDN cache.
- Treating the cache as the source of truth for critical data.

activity.prompt: Match the pattern to its description.
pairs: App loads DB on miss and fills cache
Write DB only; cache on read
Cache itself loads from DB on miss

quiz.q: Most common pattern in web apps:
quiz.why: Cache-aside is the most common caching pattern in web apps because it is simple and flexible.

options: Data loss if cache fails before flush
quiz.why: Write-back risks data loss if the cache fails before the data is flushed to the database.

quiz.q: Hit ratio 80%, cache 1 ms, DB 20 ms (miss = 21 ms). Average:

quiz.why: TTL means time to live before an entry expires.
The database should be the source of truth. A cache is only a copy.

scenes.text: The cache has room for 1 million items, but there are 50 million products.
Which ones should it throw out? The eviction policy decides.

steps.title: Policies
steps.body:
- **LRU** (least recently used): evict the item unused for longest — good default.
- **LFU** (least frequently used): evict the least-used — good for stable popularity.
- **FIFO:** oldest inserted first — simple, often worse.
- **TTL-based:** expire after a time.
Redis supports policies like allkeys-lru and allkeys-lfu.

steps.title: Solved example: LRU by hand
steps.body:
Capacity 2; access A, B, A, C, B.
- A: miss → [A]
- B: miss → [A, B]
- A: hit → order [B, A]
- C: miss → evict B (least recent) → [A, C]
- B: miss → evict A → [C, B]
**Result:** hits = 1, misses = 4.

steps.title: How LRU is built
steps.body: A **hash map + doubly linked list** gives O(1) get and put: the map finds nodes; the list keeps recency order (move to front on access, evict from tail). In Python, `collections.OrderedDict` with `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)` does the same.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to update recency on a hit.
- O(n) list scans for every access.

activity.prompt: Simulate an LRU cache. Line 1: capacity. Line 2: keys accessed, space-separated. Print 'hits=H misses=M'.
activity.starter:
from collections import OrderedDict
cap = int(input())
keys = input().split()
cache = OrderedDict()
hits = misses = 0
for k in keys:
    pass  # your code
print(f'hits={hits} misses={misses}')
activity.solution:
from collections import OrderedDict
cap = int(input())
keys = input().split()
cache = OrderedDict()
hits = misses = 0
for k in keys:
    if k in cache:
        hits += 1
        cache.move_to_end(k)
    else:
        misses += 1
        cache[k] = True
        if len(cache) > cap:
            cache.popitem(last=False)
print(f'hits={hits} misses={misses}')
activity.hint: On hit: move_to_end. On miss: insert, and if over capacity popitem(last=False).

quiz.why: LRU evicts the least recently used item.
An O(1) LRU uses a hash map plus a doubly linked list, for fast lookup and fast reordering.
LFU is good when popularity is stable over time, since frequency predicts future use.

quiz.q: On a cache hit in LRU you must:
quiz.why: On a cache hit in LRU, mark the item as most recently used.

quiz.q: Capacity 1, accesses A A B A: misses =
quiz.why: With capacity 1: A misses, A hits, B misses (evicts A), A misses again. That is 3 misses.

scenes.text: Marketing cuts a phone's price, but customers still see the old price for an hour.
Then the cache entry expires at 9:00:00 and 20,000 requests hit the DB at once.

steps.title: Invalidation strategies
steps.body:
- **TTL expiry:** simple; staleness up to TTL.
- **Delete on write:** after updating DB, delete the cache key (next read refills).
- **Versioned keys:** `product:42:v7` — bump version on change.
- **Event-driven:** DB change events (CDC) invalidate caches.

steps.title: Cache stampede (thundering herd)
steps.body: When a hot key expires, many requests miss simultaneously and hammer the DB. Fixes: **request coalescing/locking** (one request rebuilds, others wait), **early refresh** before expiry, **TTL jitter** (random offsets), serve **stale-while-revalidate**.

steps.title: Solved example: update order
steps.body:
**Wrong:** delete cache, then update DB → a reader in between re-caches the old value.
**Better:** update DB, **then** delete cache. For extra safety, a short TTL limits damage if a race still happens.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Same TTL for millions of keys set at the same time → synchronized expiry storms.
- Caching errors/empty results for too long (negative caching needs short TTL).

statements.s: Adding random jitter to TTLs helps avoid synchronized expiry.
Deleting the cache before updating the DB is the safest order.
Request coalescing lets one request rebuild a hot key while others wait.
Stale-while-revalidate serves slightly old data while refreshing in the background.

options: A hot key expires and many requests miss at once
quiz.why: Thundering herd happens when a hot key expires and many requests miss at once, all hitting the database.

options: Making old entries unreachable after a change
quiz.why: Versioned keys make old entries unreachable after a change, since new data uses a new key.
TTL jitter randomises expiry times, so keys don't expire together, spreading load.
The safer order is update the DB, then delete the cache, which reduces the chance of re-caching stale data.
Negative caching ('not found') should use a short TTL, so new data isn't hidden for long.

scenes.text: An ed-tech platform serves lesson videos from one US region. Students in India wait for buffering.
With a CDN, videos are cached at edge locations near Indian cities.

steps.title: What a CDN does
steps.body: A **Content Delivery Network** caches content at many **edge locations** close to users. Benefits: lower latency, less load and egress from your origin, absorption of traffic spikes and some DDoS protection.

steps.title: Controlling caching
steps.body: HTTP headers: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400` (cache 1 day), `private` (browser only), `no-store` (don't cache). Use **content-hashed filenames** (`app.3f9a.js`) for long caching with instant updates. Invalidate (purge) on change when needed.

steps.title: Solved example: what to put on the CDN
steps.body:
✔ Images, videos, JS/CSS bundles, fonts, public downloadable PDFs.
✔ Public API responses that are the same for all users (short TTL).
✘ Personalised pages with account details (unless carefully keyed and marked private).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Caching pages with `Set-Cookie` or user data publicly → data leak.
- Long max-age on non-hashed filenames → users stuck with old files.

activity.prompt: Good for CDN caching?

items.text: Course thumbnail images
Hashed JS bundle app.3f9a.js
User's account settings page
Lesson video segments
API returning a user's bank balance

quiz.why: A CDN mainly reduces latency and load on the origin, by serving content from the edge.
Cache-Control: no-store means don't cache at all, so nothing is stored.
Content-hashed filenames allow long caching with instant updates, because new content gets a new URL.
Personal pages should be marked private or no-store, to avoid shared caching.
Edge locations are CDN servers near users, also called points of presence.

questions.q: LRU stands for:
questions.why: LRU stands for least recently used.

questions.q: CDN caches content at:
questions.why: A CDN caches content at edge locations near users.

questions.q: TTL controls:
questions.why: TTL controls expiry.

questions.q: Cache-aside on miss:
options: App reads DB and fills cache
questions.why: On a miss in cache-aside, the app reads the database and fills the cache.

questions.q: Write-through gives:
questions.why: Write-through updates the cache and DB together, giving a fresh cache but slower writes.

questions.q: Cache-Control: private means:
questions.why: Cache-Control: private means only the browser may cache the response, not shared caches like CDNs.

questions.q: Hit ratio 95%, cache 2 ms, miss total 22 ms. Average?
LRU capacity 2: A B C A — misses?
questions.why: Capacity 2, sequence A B C A: A and B miss, C evicts A, then A misses again. That gives 4 misses.

questions.q: Assertion (A): TTL jitter reduces stampedes. Reason (R): Keys stop expiring simultaneously.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: jitter stops keys expiring simultaneously, which reduces stampedes.

questions.q: Write-back is risky because:
questions.why: Write-back is risky because unflushed writes can be lost if the cache fails.

questions.q: Case: Hot key 'homepage' expires; DB CPU spikes to 100% every hour. Best fix?
questions.why: Coalesce rebuilds so only one request refreshes the key, and refresh early or serve stale-while-revalidate. This controls the stampede.

questions.q: Case: After a price update, old price shows until TTL. Lowest-effort strong fix?
options: Delete the key right after DB update (or bump version)
questions.why: Delete the key right after the DB update, or bump its version, so the cache doesn't show the old price until TTL.

questions.q: Case: CDN served one user's account page to another. Likely cause?
questions.why: A CDN serving one user's page to another means a personalised response was cached publicly. It needs private or no-store, or a correct cache key.

questions.q: Why does LRU need a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one for O(1)?
options: To remove an arbitrary node in O(1) given its pointer
questions.why: A doubly linked list lets you remove an arbitrary node in O(1) given its pointer, because it has a previous pointer.

questions.q: Case: Product catalogue with stable bestsellers and scans by bots touching each item once. Better eviction?
questions.why: With stable bestsellers and bots scanning each item once, LFU keeps the popular items, while LRU gets polluted by one-off scans.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Databases: models, indexes, replication, sharding
courses.summary: Choosing SQL or NoSQL, how indexes work, ACID and isolation, replication and consistency (CAP and PACELC), and partitioning/sharding strategies.
outcomes: Learners can choose a data model for a workload
Learners can explain B-tree indexes and their trade-offs
Learners can explain ACID and isolation anomalies
Learners can reason about replication lag and CAP/PACELC
Learners can choose shard keys and avoid hot spots

scenes.text: A team picks a document DB 'because it scales', then struggles with joins for invoices and payments.
The architect says: choose by access patterns, not hype.

steps.title: Families
steps.body:
- **Relational (SQL):** tables, schemas, joins, ACID transactions — PostgreSQL, MySQL.
- **Key-value:** get/put by key, very fast — Redis, DynamoDB.
- **Document:** JSON-like documents, flexible schema — MongoDB.
- **Wide-column:** rows with many columns, partitioned at scale — Cassandra, HBase.
- **Graph:** nodes and edges — Neo4j.
- **Time-series / search:** metrics stores, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch.

steps.title: Solved example: pick per use case
steps.body:
- Payments, orders, inventory → **SQL** (transactions, constraints).
- Session store, rate-limit counters → **key-value**.
- Product catalogue with varied attributes → **document**.
- IoT sensor readings at huge write rates → **wide-column/time-series**.
- Friend-of-friend recommendations → **graph**.
- Full-text product search → **search engine**.

steps.title: Polyglot persistence
steps.body: Large systems often use several stores, each for what it does best — with one **source of truth** per data item and pipelines to keep others in sync.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'NoSQL scales, SQL doesn't' — modern SQL scales far with replicas, partitioning and good indexing.
- Choosing schemaless and ending with inconsistent data.

activity.prompt: Match workload to store type.

quiz.why: A relational DB is the best default for financial transactions because of ACID guarantees.
Document databases store JSON-like documents with flexible structure.
Polyglot persistence means using multiple specialised stores, each fit for its purpose.
Friend-of-friend queries suit a graph database, which models relationships directly.
Choose databases primarily by access patterns and consistency needs, not popularity.

scenes.text: Login takes 9 seconds once the users table hits 50 million rows.
An index on email brings it to 3 ms.

steps.title: B-tree indexes
steps.body: Most relational indexes are **B-trees** (B+ trees): sorted, balanced trees with high fan-out. Lookup costs about **log_f(N)** page reads. With fan-out ~100 and 100M rows: log₁₀₀(10⁸) = **4 levels** — a handful of reads instead of scanning 100M rows.

steps.title: Composite and covering indexes
steps.body: Composite index (a, b) helps queries filtering on **a**, or **a and b** — the leftmost-prefix rule. It does not help a filter on **b** alone. A **covering** index includes all columns the query needs, so the table itself isn't read.

steps.title: Solved example: which index?
steps.body:
Query: `SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`.
**Index:** (user_id, created_at) — equality column first, then range/sort column. Add `total` as an included column to make it covering.

steps.title: The cost of indexes
steps.body: Every index speeds reads but **slows writes** (each insert/update must update indexes) and uses storage. Index for real query patterns; check with `EXPLAIN`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrapping indexed columns in functions (`WHERE LOWER(email)=...`) without a matching expression index.
- Leading wildcard `LIKE '%gmail.com'` can't use a normal B-tree.
- Indexing every column.

activity.prompt: Write a query that returns the name and city of customers in 'Pune', ordered by name.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Asha','Pune'),(2,'Bilal','Delhi'),(3,'Chitra','Pune'),(4,'Dev','Mumbai'),(5,'Anil','Pune'); CREATE INDEX idx_city ON customers(city);
activity.solution: SELECT name, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'Pune' ORDER BY name;

quiz.q: B-tree depth for 10⁸ rows with fan-out 100:
quiz.why: Depth ≈ log base fan-out of rows: 100⁴ = 10⁸, so a B-tree of 10⁸ rows with fan-out 100 has about 4 levels.

quiz.q: Index (a, b) helps a filter on:
quiz.why: A composite index (a, b) follows the leftmost-prefix rule, so it helps filters on a, or on a and b. It doesn't help b alone.
Indexes slow down writes, because every insert or update must also maintain the index.

options: Contains all columns the query needs
quiz.why: A covering index contains all the columns a query needs, so no table lookup is required.
LIKE '%abc' has a leading wildcard, so a B-tree index usually can't be used efficiently.

scenes.text: Two users book the last seat on a flight at the same moment.
Without proper isolation, both get confirmed.

steps.title: ACID
steps.body:
- **Atomicity:** all or nothing.
- **Consistency:** constraints hold before and after.
- **Isolation:** concurrent transactions don't interfere improperly.
- **Durability:** committed data survives crashes (write-ahead log).

steps.title: Isolation levels and anomalies
steps.body:
- **Read uncommitted:** dirty reads possible.
- **Read committed:** no dirty reads; non-repeatable reads possible.
- **Repeatable read:** same row reads stay the same; phantoms possible in the SQL standard definition.
- **Serializable:** behaves as if transactions ran one by one.
Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update, write skew.

steps.title: Solved example: the last seat
steps.body:
**Fix 1 (pessimistic):** `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the seat row; the second transaction waits, then sees it taken.
**Fix 2 (optimistic):** `UPDATE seats SET booked_by=? WHERE id=? AND booked_by IS NULL` — check affected rows = 1; if 0, someone else won.
**Fix 3:** unique constraint on (flight, seat) in bookings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Read-then-write in application code without locks or conditions → lost updates.
- Long transactions holding locks during network calls.

activity.prompt: Match the ACID letter.
pairs: Transfer debits and credits both or neither
Balance never violates a CHECK constraint

quiz.why: A dirty read means reading uncommitted data.
Serializable is the strongest isolation level, behaving as if transactions ran one after another.
Durability is usually implemented with write-ahead logging (WAL).

options: Rows affected by a conditional UPDATE
quiz.why: Optimistic seat booking checks the rows affected by a conditional UPDATE. If zero rows changed, someone else took the seat.
A lost update happens with an unprotected read-modify-write, where concurrent writes overwrite each other.

scenes.text: A user posts a comment, refreshes, and it's gone. A minute later it's back.
The read went to a replica that hadn't caught up yet: replication lag.

steps.title: Replication
steps.body: **Leader–follower:** writes go to the leader; followers copy changes and serve reads. **Synchronous** replication waits for followers (safer, slower); **asynchronous** doesn't (faster, may lose recent writes on failover, causes lag). **Read-your-writes** fix: route a user's reads to the leader for a short time after they write.

steps.title: CAP and PACELC
steps.body: **CAP:** during a network **P**artition, a distributed system must choose **C**onsistency (refuse/limit some requests) or **A**vailability (answer, maybe stale). **PACELC** adds: **E**lse (no partition), trade **L**atency vs **C**onsistency. e.g. many Dynamo-style stores are PA/EL; traditional single-leader SQL with sync replicas leans PC/EC.

steps.title: Sharding (partitioning)
steps.body:
Split data across machines by a **shard key**:
- **Range** (by date or ID range): good for range scans; risk of hot latest shard.
- **Hash** (hash of user_id): even spread; range queries harder.
- **Directory/lookup:** a map of key → shard; flexible, extra hop.
Good keys have **high cardinality** and spread **load**, and keep related data together (e.g. all of a user's orders).

steps.title: Solved example: pick a shard key
steps.body:
Chat app messages: query 'messages in conversation X, newest first'.
**Key:** conversation_id (hash) → all messages for a conversation on one shard; sort by timestamp inside.
**Avoid:** timestamp as key → all new writes hit one shard (hot spot).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sharding too early — try indexes, caching and read replicas first.
- Cross-shard joins and transactions everywhere.
- Celebrity/hot keys overwhelming one shard — add splitting or caching for them.

activity.prompt: Hash sharding demo: read user IDs (space-separated) on line 1 and shard count N on line 2. Print how many users land on each shard 0..N-1 using id % N, space-separated.
activity.starter:
ids = list(map(int, input().split()))
n = int(input())
counts = [0] * n
# fill counts
print(' '.join(map(str, counts)))
activity.solution:
ids = list(map(int, input().split()))
n = int(input())
counts = [0] * n
for i in ids:
    counts[i % n] += 1
print(' '.join(map(str, counts)))

quiz.why: Asynchronous replication can cause replication lag and stale reads, since followers may be behind.
CAP's consistency-versus-availability choice arises during a network partition.
In PACELC, 'ELC' means Else, trade latency versus consistency, during normal operation.

quiz.q: Timestamp as shard key often causes:
options: Hot spots on the latest shard
quiz.why: A timestamp as shard key often causes hot spots on the latest shard, because all new writes go together.

options: Routing the writer's reads to the leader briefly
quiz.why: Read-your-writes can be achieved by routing the writer's reads to the leader briefly, so they see fresh data.

questions.q: ACID 'A' is:
questions.why: The A in ACID is Atomicity: a transaction is all or nothing.

questions.q: Key-value stores are best for:
questions.why: Key-value stores are best for lookups by key.

questions.q: Indexes speed up:
questions.why: Indexes speed up reads.

questions.q: Followers in leader–follower replication usually serve:
questions.why: Followers in leader–follower replication usually serve reads, which scales read capacity.

questions.q: Composite index (city, age) helps:
questions.why: A composite index (city, age) helps WHERE city=? AND age>?, following the leftmost-prefix rule. It doesn't help age alone.

questions.q: Hash sharding gives:
questions.why: Hash sharding gives an even distribution but makes range scans harder.

questions.q: B-tree levels for 10⁹ rows, fan-out 1000:
questions.why: Depth ≈ 3 because 1000³ = 10⁹.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Serializable isolation prevents write skew. Reason (R): Transactions behave as if executed one after another.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: serializable isolation makes transactions behave as if executed one after another, which prevents write skew.

questions.q: Non-repeatable read means:
options: Same row read twice gives different values within a transaction
New rows appear in a range
questions.why: A non-repeatable read is when reading the same row twice in a transaction gives different values.

questions.q: Under CAP, a 'CP' system during partition:
options: May reject some requests to stay consistent
questions.why: A 'CP' system during a partition may reject some requests to stay consistent.

questions.q: Case: User updates profile, refreshes, sees old data. Fix?
options: Read-your-writes routing to leader / session consistency
questions.why: Replica lag shows old data after an update, so use read-your-writes routing to the leader or session consistency.

questions.q: Case: Orders table sharded by order_date; a big sale day overloads one shard. Better key?
questions.why: Sharding by order_date overloads one shard on a big sale day. Use a hash of customer_id or order_id to spread writes.

questions.q: Case: Query WHERE LOWER(email)=? is slow despite index on email. Fix?
options: Expression index on LOWER(email) or store normalised email
questions.why: A function on the column defeats a plain index, so use an expression index on LOWER(email) or store a normalised email.

questions.q: Case: Two doctors on-call; each checks 'at least one other on call' and goes off — both off. Anomaly?
questions.why: Two doctors each checking that someone else is on call and both leaving is write skew, a classic anomaly.

questions.q: Which is PA/EL in PACELC?
options: Dynamo-style store favouring availability and low latency
questions.why: A Dynamo-style store favouring availability and low latency is PA/EL in PACELC. A bank ledger needing linearizability is PC/EC.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Queues, streams and asynchronous processing
courses.summary: Why queues decouple systems, delivery guarantees and idempotent consumers, pub/sub and Kafka-style logs, and retries, backoff, dead-letter queues and the outbox pattern.
outcomes: Learners can explain how queues buffer and decouple
Learners can compare at-most-once, at-least-once and effectively-once processing
Learners can explain topics, partitions, offsets and consumer groups
Learners can design retries with backoff, DLQs and the outbox pattern

scenes.text: Checkout waits for the email service, the invoice PDF and the warehouse API. Any slowness makes checkout fail.
Moving those to a queue makes checkout fast and resilient.

steps.title: Decoupling
steps.body: A **producer** puts messages on a queue; **consumers** process them independently. The producer doesn't wait for or even know the consumers. If a consumer is down, messages wait safely.

steps.title: Buffering spikes
steps.body: Queues absorb bursts: 10,000 orders in a minute can be processed by workers at a steady 2,000/min. Scale workers on **queue depth**.

steps.title: Solved example: checkout redesign
steps.body:
**Synchronous part:** validate cart, charge payment, write order → return 'Order placed'.
**Async via queue (OrderPlaced event):** send email, generate invoice, notify warehouse, update analytics.
**Result:** faster checkout; a failing email service no longer blocks orders.

steps.title: Solved example: drain time
steps.body:
Backlog 120,000 messages; 20 workers × 50 msg/s = 1,000 msg/s.
**Drain time** = 120,000 / 1,000 = **120 s** (if no new arrivals).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the critical payment step on a queue without telling the user it's pending.
- No monitoring of queue age/depth → silent backlogs.

activity.prompt: Backlog 90,000 messages; 15 workers each process 40 msg/s. Seconds to drain (no new messages)?

quiz.why: A queue decouples producers from consumers, so each side works independently.
Queues help with spikes by buffering work until workers can process it.
Scale workers on queue depth or age, since backlog shows the need for more workers.

quiz.q: Which step should stay synchronous at checkout?
quiz.why: Payment authorisation and the order write should stay synchronous at checkout, since the user needs the result. Marketing emails and analytics can be async.
Drain time = 60,000 ÷ 1,000 = 60 seconds.

scenes.text: A worker sends a welcome email, then crashes before acknowledging the message.
The queue redelivers; the user gets two emails. With payments this would be serious.

steps.title: Guarantees
steps.body:
- **At-most-once:** ack before processing; may lose messages, never duplicates.
- **At-least-once:** ack after processing; never lose, may **duplicate** (most common).
- **Exactly-once processing:** in practice achieved as **at-least-once + idempotent processing** (or transactional systems that commit output and offsets together).

steps.title: Idempotent consumers
steps.body: Give each message a unique ID. Before processing, check a **processed-IDs** store (or use a unique constraint); skip if seen. Or make the operation naturally idempotent (`SET status='PAID'` rather than `balance = balance - 100`).

steps.title: Solved example: dedupe
steps.body:
Messages arrive: m1, m2, m1, m3, m2.
Seen-set: {} → m1 process → {m1} → m2 process → {m1,m2} → m1 skip → m3 process → m2 skip.
**Processed 3, duplicates 2.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the queue guarantees no duplicates.
- Incrementing counters on each delivery.
- Keeping the dedupe store forever with no TTL/size plan.

activity.prompt: Read message IDs (space-separated). Process each unique ID once. Print 'processed=P duplicates=D'.
activity.starter:
ids = input().split()
seen = set()
processed = duplicates = 0
# your code
print(f'processed={processed} duplicates={duplicates}')
activity.hint: Use a set of seen IDs.

quiz.why: At-least-once is the most common delivery guarantee, a safe default, though it can cause duplicates.
At-least-once delivery requires idempotent consumers, to handle duplicates safely.
SET status='SHIPPED' is naturally idempotent, since repeating it gives the same result. Counters and appends change each time.
At-most-once acknowledges before processing, so a crash can lose the message.
Effectively-once is commonly built from at-least-once delivery plus deduplication.

scenes.text: An 'OrderPlaced' event is needed by billing, shipping, fraud and analytics teams.
A log-based stream lets each team read at its own pace — and replay history.

steps.title: Queue vs pub/sub
steps.body:
- **Queue (point-to-point):** each message is handled by **one** consumer among workers.
- **Pub/sub:** each message goes to **every** subscriber group.
Kafka combines both: **consumer groups** each get all messages; within a group, partitions are split among members.

steps.title: Kafka concepts
steps.body:
- **Topic:** named stream of records.
- **Partition:** ordered, append-only log; ordering is guaranteed **within a partition only**.
- **Key:** records with the same key go to the same partition (e.g. order_id → per-order ordering).
- **Offset:** position of a record; consumers commit offsets.
- **Consumer group:** at most one consumer per partition in a group → max parallelism = number of partitions.
- **Retention:** records kept for a time/size, enabling **replay**.

steps.title: Solved example: parallelism
steps.body: Topic with **6 partitions**; group with **8 consumers** → only 6 are active, 2 idle. To use 8, increase partitions (plan ahead — changing partition count remaps keys).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting global ordering across partitions.
- Random keys when per-entity order matters.
- Too few partitions for future scale.

statements.s: Kafka guarantees ordering across all partitions of a topic.
Records with the same key go to the same partition (default partitioner).
In one consumer group, a partition is consumed by at most one member at a time.
Retention allows consumers to replay old events.

quiz.q: Max active consumers in a group for a 12-partition topic:
quiz.why: In a consumer group, at most one active consumer per partition, so a 12-partition topic supports 12 active consumers.
Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition, not across partitions or topics.

options: A record's position in a partition
quiz.why: An offset is a record's position in a partition.
Pub/sub delivers each message to every subscriber group.

quiz.q: To keep all events of one order in order, key by:
quiz.why: Key by order_id so all events of one order go to the same partition and stay in order.

lessons.title: Retries, backoff, DLQs and the outbox pattern

scenes.text: A partner API slows down; 5,000 workers retry instantly and endlessly.
The partner goes fully down. Backoff with jitter and a dead-letter queue would have prevented it.

steps.title: Exponential backoff with jitter
steps.body: Wait longer after each failure: base × 2^attempt (e.g. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 s), capped, plus **random jitter** so clients don't retry in sync. Retry only **transient** errors (timeouts, 503, 429); don't retry 400-type validation errors.

steps.title: Dead-letter queue (DLQ)
steps.body: After N failed attempts, move the message to a **DLQ** for inspection, so one 'poison' message doesn't block or loop forever. Alert on DLQ growth.

steps.title: Transactional outbox
steps.body: Problem: write to DB **and** publish an event — one may succeed and the other fail. **Outbox:** in the same DB transaction, write the business row **and** an 'outbox' row; a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes, marking rows sent. Consumers stay idempotent because the relay may publish twice.

steps.title: Solved example: backoff schedule
steps.body: Base 1 s, factor 2, cap 30 s, 6 retries: waits 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 30 (capped from 32) → total wait ≈ **61 s** before the message goes to the DLQ (plus jitter).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Immediate infinite retries.
- Retrying non-idempotent operations without keys.
- 'Dual writes' to DB and broker without an outbox.

activity.prompt: Order the outbox flow.
items: Insert OrderPlaced row into outbox table
Relay publishes to the broker and marks rows sent

quiz.why: Jitter prevents synchronised retry storms, by randomising retry timing.

quiz.q: Should you retry HTTP 400 validation errors?
quiz.why: Don't retry HTTP 400 validation errors, since the same bad request will keep failing.
A DLQ (dead-letter queue) holds messages that repeatedly failed, such as poison messages.
The outbox pattern solves dual-write inconsistency, by recording the event atomically with the data change.

questions.q: A queue's main benefit:
questions.why: A queue's main benefit is decoupling and buffering.

questions.q: DLQ stands for:
questions.why: DLQ stands for dead-letter queue.

questions.q: Kafka ordering is per:
questions.why: Kafka ordering is per partition.

questions.q: At-least-once may cause:
questions.why: At-least-once delivery may cause duplicates, because messages can be redelivered.

questions.q: Exponential backoff waits:
questions.why: Exponential backoff waits increasingly longer between retries.

questions.q: Consumer group parallelism is limited by:
questions.why: Consumer group parallelism is limited by the number of partitions, one consumer per partition.

questions.q: Backlog 200,000; 25 workers × 80 msg/s. Drain time?
questions.why: 25 workers × 80 msg/s = 2,000 msg/s, so the drain time is 200,000 ÷ 2,000 = 100 s.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Idempotent consumers make at-least-once safe. Reason (R): Processing a duplicate has no additional effect.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: processing a duplicate has no extra effect for idempotent consumers, which makes at-least-once safe.

questions.q: Which is naturally idempotent?
options: Upsert by primary key with same values
questions.why: An upsert by primary key with the same values gives the same final state, so it is naturally idempotent. Sending an SMS, incrementing and appending are not.

questions.q: Pub/sub differs from a work queue because:
options: Each subscriber group gets every message
questions.why: Pub/sub differs from a work queue because each subscriber group gets every message (fan-out).

questions.q: Case: Service writes order to DB then publishes event; broker down → order saved, no event. Fix?
questions.why: Use a transactional outbox: write the event with the order in one DB transaction and publish it later. This fixes the dual-write problem.

questions.q: Case: Events for the same account processed out of order. Likely cause and fix?
options: Random partition keys → key by account_id
questions.why: Random partition keys scatter an account's events across partitions, so ordering is lost. Key by account_id to keep them in one partition.

questions.q: Case: One malformed message crashes consumers repeatedly, blocking a partition. Fix?
options: Retry limit then DLQ, with alerting
questions.why: A malformed 'poison' message should be retried a limited number of times, then moved to a DLQ with alerting, so it stops blocking the partition.

questions.q: Backoff base 0.5 s, factor 2, cap 8 s, 7 attempts in total: total waiting time between attempts (no jitter)?
questions.why: 7 attempts have 6 waits: 0.5 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 8 (capped at 8) = 23.5 s.

questions.q: Why can't 'exactly-once' be guaranteed by the network alone?
options: A sender can't distinguish a lost message from a lost acknowledgement, so it must retry, risking duplicates
questions.why: A sender can't tell a lost message from a lost acknowledgement, so it must retry and may create duplicates. That is why exactly-once can't be guaranteed by the network alone.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Case studies: shortener, rate limiter, feed, chat
courses.summary: Four classic end-to-end designs worked step by step: URL shortener, rate limiter, news feed and real-time chat.
outcomes: Learners can design a URL shortener with ID generation and caching
Learners can implement and place a token-bucket rate limiter
Learners can choose fan-out on write vs read for feeds
Learners can design a chat system with WebSockets, ordering and delivery receipts

scenes.text: A marketing team needs short links for 100 million campaign URLs per month.
How long must the code be, and how do we avoid collisions?

steps.title: Requirements and estimates
steps.body: Writes: 100M/month ≈ 40/s average. Reads 100× → ~4,000/s. 5 years ≈ 6 billion links. Each record ~500 B → ~3 TB.

steps.title: Code length
steps.body: Base62 (0–9, a–z, A–Z) gives 62ⁿ codes. 62⁶ ≈ 5.7 × 10¹⁰ (57 billion) > 6 billion ✔; 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 × 10¹² for growth.

steps.title: ID generation options
steps.body:
- **Counter + base62:** unique, short; needs a distributed ID service (ranges handed to each server, or a Snowflake-style ID).
- **Hash (e.g. of URL) truncated:** may collide → check and retry.
- **Random code + uniqueness check:** simple; check-and-insert with a unique constraint.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.body: API servers → ID generator → key-value/SQL store (code → long URL, unique index) → cache (Redis) for hot codes → CDN/edge for redirects. Use **301** (permanent, cached by browsers) or **302** (temporary, every click hits you — better for analytics).

steps.title: Solved example: base62
steps.body:
Encode 125: 125 ÷ 62 = 2 remainder 1 → digits (2, 1) → '21'.
Encode 3,844 = 62² → '100'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sequential codes reveal volume and allow enumeration — add obfuscation if that matters.
- Forgetting abuse: malware links, spam — add scanning and rate limits.

activity.prompt: Encode a non-negative integer in base62 using the alphabet 0-9, a-z, A-Z. Print the code.
activity.starter:
ALPHA = '0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'
n = int(input())
# build the code
activity.hint: Repeatedly divmod by 62 and prepend ALPHA[r].

quiz.why: 62⁶ ≈ 5.68 × 10¹⁰, which is about 57 billion.
Use 302 for analytics, because browsers don't cache it, so each click reaches your server. A 301 is cached.
For collisions in hashed codes, check and retry or extend the code. Overwriting would send users to the wrong URL.
When reads far exceed writes, cache hot codes.
In base62, 62 = 1 × 62 + 0, so it is written '10'.

scenes.text: A buggy client script calls the public API 50,000 times a minute.
A rate limiter returns 429 to that client and keeps the service healthy for everyone else.

steps.title: Algorithms
steps.body:
- **Token bucket:** bucket holds up to C tokens, refilled at R/s; each request takes one → allows bursts up to C, average R.
- **Leaky bucket:** requests processed at a fixed rate; smooths bursts.
- **Fixed window counter:** count per minute; simple; burst at window edges.
- **Sliding window log/counter:** more accurate, a bit more cost.

steps.title: Where and how
steps.body: At the API gateway or a middleware layer. Key by API key/user/IP. Store counters in Redis with atomic operations (INCR with expiry, or Lua scripts). Return **429** with a `Retry-After` header; expose limits in headers.

steps.title: Solved example: token bucket trace
steps.body:
C = 2, R = 1/s, bucket full at t=0. Requests at t = 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 3:
- t0: 2→1 ✔, 1→0 ✔, 0 ✘
- t1: +1 → 1 → 0 ✔; next ✘
- t3: +2 → 2 (cap) → 1 ✔
**Result:** A A D A D A

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Non-atomic read-then-write counters → limits exceeded under concurrency.
- Per-server in-memory limits behind a load balancer → effective limit × N servers.
- Fixed windows allowing 2× bursts at the boundary.

activity.prompt: Token bucket. Line 1: capacity C and refill rate R (tokens per second). Line 2: request timestamps (integer seconds, non-decreasing). Bucket starts full at time 0. For each request print A (allowed) or D (denied) with no spaces.
activity.starter:
C, R = map(int, input().split())
ts = list(map(int, input().split()))
tokens, last = C, 0
out = ''
for t in ts:
    pass  # refill, then allow or deny
print(out)
activity.solution:
C, R = map(int, input().split())
ts = list(map(int, input().split()))
tokens, last = C, 0
out = ''
for t in ts:
    tokens = min(C, tokens + (t - last) * R)
    last = t
    if tokens >= 1:
        tokens -= 1
        out += 'A'
    else:
        out += 'D'
print(out)
activity.hint: tokens = min(C, tokens + (t - last) * R) before each decision.

quiz.q: Token bucket allows bursts up to:
quiz.why: A token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity C, the stored tokens.
HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) is the code for rate-limited requests.
A fixed window's weakness is bursts at window boundaries, which can allow double the limit.

quiz.q: Distributed limits are usually stored in:
quiz.why: Distributed limits are usually stored in Redis with atomic operations, which is shared, fast and atomic.

quiz.q: Per-server in-memory limits with 5 servers allow up to:
quiz.why: Per-server in-memory limits with 5 servers aren't shared, so users could reach 5× the intended limit.

scenes.text: A famous cricketer with 40 million followers posts a photo.
If we write it into 40 million feeds instantly, the system chokes. If we compute every feed on read, timelines are slow.

steps.title: Fan-out on write (push)
steps.body: When a user posts, write the post ID into each follower's precomputed feed (in Redis/wide-column). **Reads are fast.** Costly for users with huge follower counts.

steps.title: Fan-out on read (pull)
steps.body: Build the feed at read time by fetching recent posts from everyone you follow and merging. **Writes are cheap**; reads are heavier.

steps.title: Hybrid
steps.body: Push for normal users; **pull for celebrities** (their posts merged in at read time). Cache feeds; store only post IDs in feeds and hydrate details from a post cache; rank with a scoring service; paginate with cursors.

steps.title: Solved example: cost of push
steps.body: Average user: 200 followers; 50M posts/day → 10¹⁰ feed inserts/day ≈ **116,000 writes/s** on average. A single 40M-follower post would add 40M writes alone — hence pull for celebrities.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Storing full post objects in each feed (huge duplication).
- Ignoring deletions/privacy changes that must propagate to feeds.

activity.prompt: Push (fan-out on write) or pull (fan-out on read)?

items.text: Normal user with 300 followers posts
Celebrity with 30M followers posts
Need the fastest possible feed reads for most users
Inactive users who rarely open the app

quiz.why: Fan-out on write precomputes feeds, so reads are fast but writes are heavy.
Celebrities are usually handled by pulling their posts at read time, to avoid huge fan-out on write.
Feeds should store post IDs, not full content, to avoid duplication.
Feed pagination should use cursors, which stay stable as new posts arrive.
10¹⁰ ÷ 86,400 ≈ 116,000 inserts per second.

scenes.text: Users expect messages instantly, in order, with sent/delivered/read ticks — even after their train goes through a tunnel.
The design centres on persistent connections and a durable message store.

steps.title: Connections
steps.body: Clients keep a **WebSocket** (or similar long-lived connection) to a **chat gateway**. A presence/session service records which gateway each user is connected to (e.g. in Redis).

steps.title: Send path
steps.body: 1) Sender → gateway → chat service. 2) Assign a per-conversation **sequence number**; persist to the message store (wide-column keyed by conversation_id, ordered by sequence). 3) Ack 'sent' to sender. 4) Look up recipient's gateway; push. 5) Recipient acks → 'delivered'; on open → 'read'. If offline → store and send **push notification**; client syncs from its last sequence number on reconnect.

steps.title: Groups
steps.body: Small groups: fan-out to each member's connection. Large groups/channels: fan-out via a pub/sub per channel. Media goes to object storage; messages carry links.

steps.title: Solved example: reconnect after tunnel
steps.body: Client last saw seq 1,042 in conversation C. On reconnect it asks: 'give me C after 1,042' → server returns 1,043–1,050 in order. Client-generated message IDs make resend idempotent (no duplicates if the 'sent' ack was lost).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using wall-clock timestamps from devices for ordering.
- Polling every second instead of persistent connections.
- No idempotency for resends → duplicate messages.

activity.prompt: Order the one-to-one message flow.
items: Sender sends over WebSocket to gateway
Chat service assigns conversation sequence number
Message pushed to recipient's gateway (or push notification if offline)

quiz.why: Chat clients usually use WebSockets or other long-lived connections for real-time push.

quiz.q: Ordering within a conversation is best done with:
quiz.why: Server-assigned sequence numbers give a monotonic order per conversation. Device clocks can drift.
Offline recipients get stored messages plus a push notification, so they receive them when back online.
Client-generated message IDs make resends idempotent, since the server can drop duplicates.
Partition the message store by conversation_id so a chat's messages stay together.

questions.q: Base62 uses:
questions.why: Base62 uses 62 symbols: 0–9, a–z and A–Z.

questions.q: Rate-limit response code:
questions.why: The rate-limit response code is 429, Too Many Requests.

questions.q: Chat real-time delivery typically uses:
questions.why: Chat real-time delivery typically uses WebSockets, which are persistent connections.

questions.q: Fan-out on read is good for:
questions.why: Fan-out on read is good for celebrity posts, avoiding huge writes.

questions.q: Token bucket average rate equals:
questions.why: A token bucket's long-run average rate equals the refill rate R.

questions.q: 301 redirects are:
questions.why: 301 redirects are permanent and cacheable, so browsers remember them.

questions.q: Base62 of 125:
questions.why: 125 = 2 × 62 + 1, so in base62 it is '21'.

questions.q: Min base62 length for 6 billion unique codes:
questions.why: 62⁵ ≈ 9.2 × 10⁸, which is below 6 × 10⁹, while 62⁶ ≈ 5.7 × 10¹⁰ is enough. So you need 6 characters.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Per-server rate limits behind an LB can be exceeded globally. Reason (R): Each server counts independently.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: each server counts independently, so limits can be exceeded globally, which is why a shared store is needed.

questions.q: Token bucket C=3, R=1, requests at 0,0,0,0,2: result?
questions.why: With C=3, R=1: requests at t=0 use 3 tokens, the 4th is denied. At t=2, 2 tokens have refilled, so the 5th is allowed. Result AAADA.

questions.q: Case: Feed writes overwhelm Redis whenever a star posts. Fix?
options: Hybrid: pull celebrity posts at read time
questions.why: Use a hybrid approach: push for normal users and pull celebrity posts at read time. This avoids a write storm when a star posts.

questions.q: Case: Chat shows messages out of order after reconnect. Fix?
options: Server sequence numbers per conversation and sync from last seq
questions.why: Use server sequence numbers per conversation and sync from the last sequence after reconnecting. Device time or alphabetical sorting is unreliable.

questions.q: Case: Short codes from truncated hashes sometimes collide. Fix?
options: Unique constraint; on conflict, add salt/extend and retry
questions.why: Put a unique constraint on the code, and on conflict add a salt or extend it and retry. Overwriting would send users to the wrong URL.

questions.q: Case: Average 200 followers, 20M posts/day with push. Avg feed writes per second?
questions.why: 20M posts × 200 followers = 4 × 10⁹ writes a day, and ÷ 86,400 ≈ 46,000 per second.

questions.q: Why is a sliding-window counter more accurate than a fixed window?
options: It weights the previous window, avoiding 2× bursts at boundaries
questions.why: A sliding-window counter weights the previous window, which avoids 2× bursts at fixed-window boundaries.

courses.title: System design · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: A one-page formula and pattern sheet, an interview framework drill, and a full mock test across all chapters.
outcomes: Learners can recall key numbers and formulas
Learners can run a 45-minute design interview structure
Learners can score 80%+ on the mock

scenes.text: Ritika has a system design round tomorrow.
She revises from one compact sheet.

steps.title: Numbers
steps.body:
- 1 day ≈ 10⁵ s; QPS = daily requests / 86,400; peak ≈ 2–3×
- Nines: 99.9% → 8.76 h/yr; 99.99% → 52.6 min/yr
- Series availability = product; parallel = 1 − ∏(1 − aᵢ)
- Cache average = h·t_cache + (1−h)·t_miss
- B-tree levels ≈ log_fanout(N)
- Modulo remap moves ≈ N/(N+1); consistent hashing ≈ 1/N
- 62⁶ ≈ 5.7×10¹⁰; 62⁷ ≈ 3.5×10¹²

steps.title: Patterns
steps.body: Stateless + LB · cache-aside + TTL + jitter · CDN with hashed assets · read replicas · shard by high-cardinality key · queue + idempotent consumers · outbox · backoff + jitter + DLQ · token bucket · hybrid feed fan-out · WebSockets + sequence numbers

steps.title: Top mistakes
steps.body: No requirements · averages not percentiles · single points of failure · stale cache invalidation order · hot shard keys · non-idempotent retries · dual writes

quiz.why: Two replicas in parallel fail only if both fail: 0.001 × 0.001 = 10⁻⁶, so availability is 99.9999%.
Exactly-once in practice is built from at-least-once delivery plus idempotency.
8.64 × 10⁸ ÷ 86,400 = 10,000 requests per second.
A timestamp is a hot shard key, since all new writes land on the latest shard.

scenes.text: Practice prompt: match riders to nearby drivers in real time.
Use the framework, 45 minutes.

steps.title: Framework (45 min)
steps.body:
1) **Requirements** (5 min) — functional, non-functional, scope.
2) **Estimates** (5 min) — QPS, storage, bandwidth.
3) **API** (5 min).
4) **High-level design** (10 min) — boxes and arrows.
5) **Deep dives** (15 min) — data model, scaling, bottlenecks.
6) **Wrap-up** (5 min) — trade-offs, failure modes, monitoring.

steps.title: Worked sketch: dispatch
steps.body:
**Req:** riders request; nearest available driver within 2 km gets offer; < 1 s matching.
**Estimate:** 1M active drivers sending location every 4 s → 250,000 writes/s.
**Design:** location updates → in-memory geo index (geohash/grid cells, e.g. Redis geo) sharded by region; matching service queries nearby cells; offers via push/WebSocket; trips in SQL (transactions).
**Deep dive:** hot cells at airports → finer cells; driver locks with TTL to avoid double assignment.

steps.title: Talk trade-offs
steps.body: Every choice has a cost. Say it: 'I chose eventual consistency for location because a 4-second lag is acceptable; trips use strong consistency.'

activity.prompt: Order the interview framework.

quiz.why: 1 million drivers every 4 seconds gives 10⁶ ÷ 4 = 250,000 writes per second.
Trips need strong consistency and transactions, because they involve money and assignment.
A geo index commonly uses geohash or grid cells, which bucket space for fast lookup.
The last step of the framework is trade-offs and failure modes, as a wrap-up.

scenes.text: Do the 20-question mock in 25 minutes.
Redo any chapter where you missed two or more.

steps.title: Numericals
steps.body: Write the formula first, round to powers of ten, then compute. Check units (bytes vs bits, seconds vs days).

steps.title: Case questions
steps.body: Identify the bottleneck (CPU, DB, network, hot key, coordination) before choosing the fix.

steps.title: Next steps
steps.body: Re-implement the code tasks from memory: LRU, token bucket, base62, dedupe consumer.

activity.prompt: Which system design topic is weakest for you, and what will you build or read this week to fix it?
activity.hint: e.g. 'Sharding — I'll design shard keys for three apps.'

quiz.why: On a numerical, first write the formula, to structure your working.
Before choosing a fix, identify the bottleneck. Adding servers or caches blindly may not help.
Units.

questions.q: QPS for 10⁸ requests/day ≈
questions.why: 10⁸ ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1,160 requests per second.

questions.q: L7 LB can route by:
questions.why: An L7 load balancer can route by URL path, because it understands HTTP.

questions.q: LRU evicts:
questions.why: LRU evicts the least recently used item.

questions.q: Most common delivery guarantee:
questions.why: At-least-once is the most common delivery guarantee, the default in most systems.

questions.q: Read replicas help with:
questions.why: Read replicas help with read scaling by spreading reads across followers.

questions.q: CDN best for:
questions.why: A CDN is best for static assets and media, which are cacheable.

questions.q: Idempotent HTTP method:
questions.why: DELETE is idempotent: repeating it has the same effect. POST isn't.

questions.q: Composite index (a,b) helps filter on b alone?
questions.why: A composite index (a, b) doesn't help filter on b alone, by the leftmost-prefix rule.

questions.q: Three 99.9% services in series ≈
questions.why: Three 99.9% services in series: 0.999³ ≈ 0.997, about 99.7%.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Async replication can lose recent writes on failover. Reason (R): Followers may lag behind the leader.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: followers may lag behind the leader, so async replication can lose recent writes on failover.

questions.q: Consumers > partitions in a group means:
questions.why: With more consumers than partitions, some consumers are idle, since each partition has one consumer.

questions.q: Cache h=0.9, cache 1 ms, miss 31 ms. Average?
Case: Adding a cache node empties the cache (modulo hashing). Fix?
questions.why: Use consistent hashing with virtual nodes, so adding a cache node remaps only a small share of keys instead of emptying the cache.

questions.q: Case: Payment retried after timeout, customer charged twice. Fix?
questions.why: An idempotency key makes retries safe, so the payment is processed only once.

questions.q: Case: Hot key expiry spikes DB each hour. Fix?
questions.why: Coalescing rebuilds, early refresh and TTL jitter prevent the hourly stampede on the DB.

questions.q: Case: DB write succeeds, event publish fails. Pattern?
questions.why: If the DB write succeeds but the event publish fails, use the outbox pattern to publish reliably.

questions.q: Peak 40,000 RPS, 250 RPS per instance, 25% headroom → instances?
questions.why: 40,000 ÷ 250 = 160 instances, and with 25% headroom 160 × 1.25 = 200.

questions.q: Keys 1..60, shards 4→5 with modulo: how many move?
questions.why: A key stays only if k mod 4 equals k mod 5, which happens when k mod 20 is 0–3. In 1–60 that's 12 keys, so 48 move.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Celebrity feed → pull; normal users → push
questions.why: A hybrid feed uses pull for celebrity posts and push for normal users.

questions.q: Why are server-assigned sequence numbers better than device timestamps for chat ordering?
options: Device clocks drift/skew; the server gives a single monotonic order per conversation
questions.why: Device clocks drift and skew, while a server-assigned sequence gives a single monotonic order per conversation.

corp-tools.title: Work tools: Excel, data skills, project management and Agile/Scrum
corp-tools.description: Chapter-by-chapter practical skills for every office: Excel formulas, lookups and PivotTables, SQL for analysts with runnable queries, project management basics, and Agile and Scrum.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Excel foundations
courses.summary: Cells and references (relative, absolute, mixed), core formulas and IF, tables, formatting and validation, and text and date functions — the base for everything else. Works in Microsoft Excel and, mostly, Google Sheets.
outcomes: Learners can use relative, absolute and mixed references correctly
Learners can write SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, ROUND and IF formulas
Learners can format data as a Table with validation and conditional formatting
Learners can clean text and work with dates using common functions

scenes.text: Rhea calculates sales commission at 5% in cell B1 and copies her formula down. Every row after the first shows 0.
Her colleague adds two dollar signs and the sheet works.

steps.title: Formulas start with =
steps.body: A formula begins with **=**: `=A2*B1`. Operators: + − * / ^ (power). Excel follows the usual order: brackets, powers, × ÷, + −. `=2+3*4` gives 14; `=(2+3)*4` gives 20.

steps.title: Reference types
steps.body:
- **Relative** `A2`: changes when copied (A2 → A3 when copied down).
- **Absolute** `$B$1`: never changes.
- **Mixed** `$A2` (column fixed) or `A$2` (row fixed).
Press **F4** (Windows) while editing a reference to cycle through types.

steps.title: Solved example: Rhea's fix
steps.body:
Rate in **B1**; sales in A4:A20.
**Wrong:** `=A4*B1` copied down becomes `=A5*B2`, `=A6*B3`… (empty cells → 0).
**Right:** `=A4*$B$1` copied down becomes `=A5*$B$1` ✔.

steps.title: Solved example: a multiplication table with mixed refs
steps.body: Numbers 1–9 in B1:J1 (across) and A2:A10 (down). In B2 type `=$A2*B$1` and fill right and down. Column A and row 1 stay locked correctly, building the whole table from one formula.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Typing numbers into formulas (`=A4*0.05`) instead of referencing an input cell — hard to update.
- Forgetting `$` for a fixed rate.
- Numbers stored as text (left-aligned, green triangle) — convert them before calculating.

activity.prompt: Complete the formula so the tax rate in cell C1 stays fixed when copied down.

quiz.why: Multiplication comes before addition, so 2 + 3 × 4 = 2 + 12 = 14.
$B$1 is an absolute reference, with both column and row locked.

quiz.q: A2 copied one row down becomes:
quiz.why: Copying A2 one row down gives A3, since a relative reference shifts with the copy.
F4 cycles through reference types (absolute, mixed, relative) in Windows Excel.
$A2 is a mixed reference that locks column A only, while the row can change.

scenes.text: A training coordinator has 200 scores and needs averages, counts and pass/fail labels by noon.
Five functions do it in ten minutes.

steps.title: Everyday functions
steps.body:
- `=SUM(B2:B201)` total
- `=AVERAGE(B2:B201)` mean
- `=COUNT(B2:B201)` count of numbers; `=COUNTA(A2:A201)` count of non-empty cells; `=COUNTBLANK(...)`
- `=MIN(...)`, `=MAX(...)`
- `=ROUND(B2,1)` round to 1 decimal; `ROUNDUP`, `ROUNDDOWN`

steps.title: IF
steps.body:
`=IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)`
Example: `=IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail")`. Comparison operators: = <> > < >= <=. Text in formulas goes in double quotes.

steps.title: Solved example: scores
steps.body:
Scores: 35, 62, 48, 90, 40.
- SUM = 275; AVERAGE = 55; MAX = 90; MIN = 35
- `=IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail")` → Fail, Pass, Pass, Pass, Pass
- `=COUNTIF(B2:B6,">=40")` → 4 passes

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using COUNT on text cells (returns 0) — use COUNTA.
- Forgetting quotes around text results.
- Formatting to show fewer decimals doesn't change the stored value; use ROUND when the value itself must change.

activity.prompt: Scores 40, 70, 55, 85, 50. What is =AVERAGE of these?

quiz.why: COUNTA counts non-empty cells, whatever they contain.
With A1 = 50, the test A1>=50 is true because >= includes 50, so it returns "Yes".
ROUND(3.456,1) rounds to one decimal place, giving 3.5.
The not-equal operator in Excel is <>.
Text results in formulas need double quotes.

scenes.text: Every month, Arjun adds rows to his sales sheet and his totals miss the new rows.
Converting the range to an Excel Table fixes it permanently.

steps.title: Excel Tables (Ctrl+T)
steps.body: A Table auto-expands as you add rows, keeps formatting consistent, adds filter buttons, and uses **structured references** like `=SUM(Sales[Amount])` that are readable and grow automatically.

steps.title: Data validation
steps.body: Data → Data Validation: restrict entries to a list (dropdown), whole numbers in a range, dates, or custom rules — preventing typos like 'Nroth' for 'North'.

steps.title: Conditional formatting
steps.body: Home → Conditional Formatting: highlight values above a threshold, duplicates, top 10, data bars or colour scales. Example: highlight overdue dates `=C2<TODAY()` in red.

steps.title: Solved example: a clean tracker
steps.body: 1) Ctrl+T to make a Table named Tasks. 2) Status column validation: list 'Not started, In progress, Done'. 3) Conditional format: Due date < TODAY() and Status <> Done → red. 4) Total open: `=COUNTIFS(Tasks[Status],"<>Done")`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Merged cells inside data — they break sorting and filtering.
- Blank rows in the middle of data.
- Several header rows; use one header row.

activity.prompt: Match the feature to its use.

quiz.why: Ctrl+T creates a Table in Excel.
=SUM(Sales[Amount]) uses a structured reference, which is Table syntax.
Use data validation with a list rule to create a dropdown.
Merged cells in data break sorting and filtering, so avoid them.

quiz.q: Highlight overdue dates with the rule:
quiz.why: To highlight overdue dates use =C2<TODAY(), which is true for dates earlier than today.

scenes.text: An HR export has names with extra spaces, codes like 'EMP-00123', and joining dates.
Text and date functions tidy it in minutes.

steps.title: Text functions
steps.body:
- `TRIM(A2)` removes extra spaces
- `UPPER`, `LOWER`, `PROPER`
- `LEFT(A2,3)`, `RIGHT(A2,5)`, `MID(A2,5,3)`
- `LEN(A2)` length; `FIND("-",A2)` position
- `A2&" "&B2` or `CONCAT` / `TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,A2:C2)`
- `TEXT(B2,"dd-mmm-yyyy")` format a number/date as text

steps.title: Date functions
steps.body:
Dates are stored as serial numbers, so you can subtract them.
- `TODAY()`, `DATE(2026,4,1)`
- `YEAR`, `MONTH`, `DAY`
- `EOMONTH(B2,0)` last day of the month
- `NETWORKDAYS(start,end,holidays)` working days (Mon–Fri) excluding listed holidays
- `EDATE(B2,6)` same day six months later

steps.title: Solved example: employee code
steps.body:
A2 = 'EMP-00123'.
- Number part: `=RIGHT(A2,5)` → '00123'; as number `=VALUE(RIGHT(A2,5))` → 123
- Prefix: `=LEFT(A2,FIND("-",A2)-1)` → 'EMP'

steps.title: Solved example: days of service
steps.body: Joined 15-Jan-2024, today 15-Jan-2026: `=TODAY()-B2` → 731 days (2024 is a leap year). Years completed: `=DATEDIF(B2,TODAY(),"y")` → 2 (DATEDIF works in Excel though it isn't listed in the function wizard).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dates stored as text (e.g. imported '01.04.2026') — convert before calculating.
- Mixing dd/mm and mm/dd formats from different systems.
- Using TEXT() results in maths — they're text.

questions.why: Every Excel formula starts with the = sign.

outcomes: Learners can write exact-match VLOOKUPs and explain their limits

scenes.text: An invoice shows the wrong price because a VLOOKUP returned the nearest match instead of the exact one.
One missing argument — FALSE — caused it.

steps.title: Syntax
steps.body:
`=VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup])`
- Looks in the **first column** of table_array, returns the value from column number col_index_num.
- **range_lookup = FALSE (or 0)** for exact match. If omitted, Excel assumes approximate match (TRUE), which needs sorted data and can return wrong results.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Price list in E2:G100 (Code | Name | Price). Code in A2.
`=VLOOKUP(A2,$E$2:$G$100,3,FALSE)` → price for that code. Lock the table with `$` before copying down.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body:
- Can't look **left** (lookup column must be first).
- Column index breaks if someone inserts a column.
- Returns #N/A when not found — wrap with IFERROR if needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Omitting FALSE.
- Not locking table_array.
- Extra spaces or text-vs-number codes ('00123' vs 123) causing #N/A — clean with TRIM/VALUE.

activity.prompt: Complete for an exact match returning the 2nd column.

options: The first column of the table
quiz.why: VLOOKUP searches in the first (leftmost) column of the table.
For an exact match, the last argument is FALSE or 0.
VLOOKUP can't look to the left of its lookup column, which is a known limitation.
#N/A from VLOOKUP usually means the value was not found.

quiz.why: The answer is "Break the column index". Reason: Hard-coded index. The other choices, such as "Do nothing" and "Fix errors", do not fit the question. (Question: Inserting a column inside the table can:)

scenes.text: Priya needs an employee's ID, which sits to the left of the name column. VLOOKUP can't do it.
XLOOKUP (and the classic INDEX/MATCH) can.

steps.title: XLOOKUP
steps.body:
`=XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode])`
Exact match by default, looks in any direction, has a built-in 'not found' value. Available in Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021+ (and in Google Sheets).

steps.title: INDEX/MATCH
steps.body: `=INDEX(return_range, MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_range, 0))` — MATCH finds the position (0 = exact), INDEX returns the value at that position. Works in all Excel versions, any direction, and doesn't break when columns are inserted.

steps.title: Solved example: ID to the left
steps.body:
IDs in A2:A500, names in B2:B500, name to find in E2.
**XLOOKUP:** `=XLOOKUP(E2,B2:B500,A2:A500,"Not found")`
**INDEX/MATCH:** `=INDEX(A2:A500,MATCH(E2,B2:B500,0))`

steps.title: Solved example: two-way lookup
steps.body:
Sales grid: regions in A2:A5, months in B1:M1. Find Region in P1 and Month in P2:
`=INDEX(B2:M5, MATCH(P1,A2:A5,0), MATCH(P2,B1:M1,0))`

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Lookup and return ranges of different sizes.
- Forgetting the 0 in MATCH (defaults to approximate).
- Sharing XLOOKUP files with colleagues on older Excel versions (shows #NAME?).
