scenes.text: The sales head asks: 'Total of North region orders in March above ₹10,000?'
One SUMIFS answers it — no filtering by hand.

steps.title: Syntax
steps.body:
- `=SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], …)`
- `=COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, …)`
- `=AVERAGEIFS(average_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, …)`
All criteria must be true (AND logic). Criteria can be text ("North"), comparisons (">10000"), or cell links (">="&H1).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Region in B, Date in C, Amount in D.
`=SUMIFS(D:D, B:B,"North", C:C,">="&DATE(2026,3,1), C:C,"<="&DATE(2026,3,31), D:D,">10000")`

steps.title: Solved example by hand
steps.body:
Rows: (North, 12,000), (South, 9,000), (North, 8,000), (North, 15,000).
`=SUMIFS(Amount, Region,"North", Amount,">10000")` → 12,000 + 15,000 = **27,000**
`=COUNTIFS(Region,"North")` → **3**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- SUMIF argument order differs from SUMIFS (SUMIF puts sum_range last) — prefer SUMIFS always.
- Ranges of unequal size.
- Writing ">"H1 instead of ">"&H1.

scenes.text: HR needs bonus bands: ≥90 'A', ≥75 'B', ≥60 'C', else 'D' — and blanks for missing scores.

steps.title: IFS and nested IF
steps.body: `=IFS(B2>=90,"A", B2>=75,"B", B2>=60,"C", TRUE,"D")` — conditions checked in order; TRUE acts as 'else'. Equivalent nested IF: `=IF(B2>=90,"A",IF(B2>=75,"B",IF(B2>=60,"C","D")))`.

steps.title: AND, OR, NOT
steps.body:
`=IF(AND(B2>=60,C2="Yes"),"Eligible","No")` — both true.
`=IF(OR(D2="Sick",D2="Casual"),"Leave","Present")` — either true.

steps.title: IFERROR
steps.body: `=IFERROR(VLOOKUP(A2,$E:$G,3,FALSE),"Not found")` replaces errors with a friendly value. Use it carefully — it hides **all** errors, including real mistakes.

steps.title: Solved example: bands
steps.body: Scores 92, 76, 60, 41 → A, B, C, D. Order matters: if you test ≥60 first, 92 would wrongly get 'C'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Deeply nested IFs that nobody can read — use IFS or a lookup table.
- Blanket IFERROR hiding broken formulas.

scenes.text: A CRM export has duplicates, names and cities in one column, and inconsistent spellings ('Bangalore', 'Bengaluru', 'blr').
Before any analysis, Kabir spends 20 minutes cleaning — and saves hours of wrong conclusions.

steps.title: Tools
steps.body:
- **Remove Duplicates** (Data tab) — choose which columns define a duplicate.
- **Text to Columns** — split 'Name, City' by a delimiter.
- **Flash Fill (Ctrl+E)** — type one example; Excel fills the pattern.
- **Find & Replace (Ctrl+H)** — standardise spellings.
- **TRIM/CLEAN/PROPER** — tidy text.
- **Power Query** (Data → Get & Transform) — repeatable cleaning steps you can refresh each month.

steps.title: Solved example: a cleaning checklist
steps.body: 1) Keep a copy of raw data. 2) Remove exact duplicate rows. 3) Split combined columns. 4) Standardise city names (Bangalore/blr → Bengaluru). 5) Convert text-numbers and text-dates. 6) Check blanks and outliers (e.g. age 230). 7) Document what you changed.

steps.title: Make it repeatable
steps.body: If you clean the same export every month, record the steps in Power Query once and click Refresh next time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cleaning the only copy of raw data.
- Removing 'duplicates' that are actually different orders from the same customer.
- Ignoring outliers that indicate data-entry errors.

steps.title: Building a PivotTable

steps.title: Match chart to question
steps.body:
- **Compare categories:** bar/column (sorted).
- **Trend over time:** line.
- **Part of a whole (few parts):** stacked bar or a simple pie with ≤5 slices.
- **Relationship:** scatter.
- **Distribution:** histogram/box plot.
- **Single KPI:** big number with comparison (vs target/last period).

steps.title: Design for clarity
steps.body: Clear title that states the insight ('North grew 24%, fastest of all regions'), labelled axes, start bar axes at zero, avoid 3D and clutter, highlight the key bar in a strong colour and grey the rest.

steps.title: Solved example: pick charts
steps.body:
- Monthly website visits for 2 years → line.
- Revenue by 8 products → sorted horizontal bar.
- Ad spend vs sales across 50 cities → scatter.
- Share of 3 payment modes → stacked bar or simple pie.

steps.title: Common mistakes

scenes.text: A café owner wants to know what coffee price gives ₹50,000 monthly profit.
Goal Seek finds it in seconds.

steps.title: Dynamic array functions (Microsoft 365 / Excel 2021+)
steps.body:
One formula 'spills' results into many cells:
- `=UNIQUE(B2:B500)` distinct values
- `=SORT(A2:C500,3,-1)` sort by 3rd column descending
- `=FILTER(A2:C500, B2:B500="North", "None")` rows matching a condition
- `=SORTBY`, `=SEQUENCE`
If something blocks the spill range, you see #SPILL!.

steps.title: Goal Seek
steps.body: Data → What-If Analysis → **Goal Seek**: set a formula cell to a target value by changing one input cell. For several inputs and constraints use **Solver** (add-in).

steps.title: Solved example: café
steps.body:
Profit = cups × (price − cost) − fixed. Cups 4,000, cost ₹40, fixed ₹1,30,000.
Target profit ₹50,000 → 4,000 × (P − 40) = 1,80,000 → P − 40 = 45 → **P = ₹85**. Goal Seek gives the same by changing the price cell.

scenes.text: Sales data has 8 million rows — too big for a spreadsheet.
Analyst Nisha writes three lines of SQL and gets her answer in a second.

steps.title: The basic query
steps.body:
```
SELECT column1, column2
FROM table
WHERE condition
ORDER BY column DESC;
```
- `SELECT *` returns all columns (avoid on big tables).

courses.title: Ch 5 · Project management fundamentals
courses.summary: Scope, time and cost, project life cycle, work breakdown structures and estimation, scheduling with the critical path, and managing risks, issues and stakeholders. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by PMI or AXELOS.
outcomes: Learners can explain the triple constraint and project life cycle
Learners can build a WBS and use three-point estimates
Learners can find the critical path and float

lessons.title: Triple constraint and life cycle

scenes.text: A client wants more features, the same deadline and a lower budget.
The project manager draws a triangle and explains the trade-offs.

steps.title: The triple constraint
steps.body: **Scope, time and cost** are linked, with **quality** in the middle. Change one and at least one other must change — or quality suffers. Modern guides also stress risk, resources and value.

steps.title: Project life cycle
steps.body: Initiating (charter, objectives, sponsor) → Planning (scope, schedule, budget, risks) → Executing → Monitoring & Controlling (throughout) → Closing (handover, lessons learned). **Predictive (waterfall)** plans up front; **adaptive (agile)** plans in iterations; **hybrid** mixes both.

steps.title: Solved example: a scope change
steps.body: Client adds two reports (scope ↑). Options: extend deadline by 2 weeks (time ↑), add a developer (cost ↑), or drop a lower-priority feature (scope swap). Record the decision through **change control**.

steps.title: Project charter
steps.body: Authorises the project: purpose, objectives, high-level scope, milestones, budget, sponsor, key risks, success criteria. No charter = no clear authority.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Scope creep': accepting small additions without assessing impact.
- No sponsor or unclear success criteria.
- Skipping the closing phase and lessons learned.

story.title: 'Build the app' is not a task

scenes.text: A new PM writes one task: 'Build mobile app — 3 months'. Nobody knows where to start.
Breaking it into a WBS reveals 60 manageable pieces.

steps.title: Work Breakdown Structure
steps.body: A **WBS** breaks the total scope into deliverables, then smaller **work packages** that can be estimated, assigned and tracked. The **100% rule**: the WBS includes all the work — and only the work — in scope.

steps.title: Estimation techniques
steps.body:
- **Analogous:** based on similar past projects (quick, rough).
- **Parametric:** rate × quantity (e.g. 2 days per screen × 15 screens).
- **Bottom-up:** estimate each work package and add up (most accurate, slow).
- **Three-point (PERT/beta):** E = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6, where O = optimistic, M = most likely, P = pessimistic.

steps.title: Solved example: PERT
steps.body:
Task: O = 4 days, M = 6 days, P = 14 days.
E = (4 + 4×6 + 14) ÷ 6 = (4 + 24 + 14) ÷ 6 = 42 ÷ 6 = **7 days**.
Standard deviation ≈ (P − O) ÷ 6 = 10 ÷ 6 ≈ 1.7 days.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Estimating only the 'happy path'.
- Forgetting testing, reviews, deployment and documentation.
- Treating estimates as promises — communicate ranges.

scenes.text: Two tasks are late. The PM asks: 'Does either delay the launch?'
Only one is on the critical path.

steps.title: Critical path method
steps.body: Draw tasks with durations and dependencies. The **critical path** is the **longest** path through the network; it sets the minimum project duration. Tasks on it have **zero float** — any delay delays the project. **Float (slack)** = how much a task can slip without delaying the project.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
A (3 days) → B (4) → D (2); A → C (6) → D.
Paths: A–B–D = 3+4+2 = 9; A–C–D = 3+6+2 = **11**.
**Critical path:** A–C–D, **11 days**. Float of B = 11 − 9 = **2 days**.
If B slips 1 day → no impact; if C slips 1 day → project becomes 12 days.

steps.title: Gantt charts and milestones
steps.body: A **Gantt chart** shows tasks as bars on a timeline with dependencies. **Milestones** are zero-duration checkpoints (e.g. 'UAT sign-off'). Compressing schedules: **crashing** (add resources to critical tasks, costs more) or **fast-tracking** (do tasks in parallel, adds risk).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding people to non-critical tasks to 'speed up' the project.
- Ignoring dependencies across teams.
- Forgetting that the critical path can change as tasks slip.

lessons.title: Risks, issues and the RAID log

scenes.text: A key vendor stops responding two weeks before integration.
Because the PM logged it as a risk a month ago, a backup plan is ready.

steps.title: RAID log
steps.body:
- **Risks:** uncertain future events that may affect the project (probability × impact).
- **Assumptions:** things believed true but not confirmed.
- **Issues:** problems happening now.
- **Dependencies:** things your project relies on (or that rely on it).
Each entry has an owner, date and action.

steps.title: Risk responses (threats)
steps.body:
- **Avoid** (change plan to remove it)
- **Mitigate/reduce** (lower probability or impact)
- **Transfer** (insurance, contract terms, outsourcing)
- **Accept** (actively: with contingency; or passively)
- **Escalate** (outside your authority)

steps.title: Solved example: score and respond
steps.body:
Risk: vendor delay. Probability 4/5, impact 5/5 → score **20** (high).
Response: **mitigate** — weekly vendor check-ins, a mock API so the team can keep building, and an alternative vendor shortlisted. Owner: integration lead. Review weekly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing risks (may happen) with issues (happening now).
- A risk register filled once and never reviewed.
- No owner for each risk.

steps.title: Agile Manifesto (2001): four values
steps.body:
We value:
- **Individuals and interactions** over processes and tools
- **Working software** over comprehensive documentation
- **Customer collaboration** over contract negotiation
- **Responding to change** over following a plan
'While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more.'

steps.title: A few of the 12 principles
steps.body: Satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery · welcome changing requirements · deliver working software frequently · business people and developers work together daily · working software is the primary measure of progress · sustainable pace · continuous attention to technical excellence · simplicity · self-organising teams · regular reflection and adjustment.

steps.title: Solved example: agile or not?
steps.body:
- Releasing a small feature every two weeks and gathering user feedback → agile.
- Refusing any change after sign-off → not agile.
- 60-hour weeks every sprint → violates sustainable pace.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Agile means no documentation or planning' — it means *just enough*, continuously.
- Copying ceremonies without the mindset.

steps.title: Three accountabilities (Scrum Guide 2020)
steps.body:
- **Product Owner:** maximises product value; manages and orders the **Product Backlog**; one person (not a committee).
- **Scrum Master:** accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness; coaches the team and organisation in Scrum; removes impediments.
- **Developers:** create a usable Increment each Sprint; own the Sprint Backlog.
The **Scrum Team** is typically **10 or fewer** people, with no sub-teams or hierarchies.

steps.title: Three artifacts and their commitments
steps.body:
- **Product Backlog** → commitment: **Product Goal**
- **Sprint Backlog** (Sprint Goal + selected items + plan) → commitment: **Sprint Goal**
- **Increment** → commitment: **Definition of Done**
An item is part of an Increment only when it meets the Definition of Done.

steps.title: Solved example: who does what?
steps.body:
- Re-ordering the backlog after client feedback → **Product Owner**.
- Deciding how to build the login feature → **Developers**.
- Helping the team fix long, unproductive Daily Scrums → **Scrum Master**.
- Creating a team-wide Definition of Done → the **Scrum Team** (if the organisation has one, it's the minimum).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Scrum Master acting as a project manager assigning tasks.
- A Product Owner committee.
- 'Done' meaning 'coded but not tested'.

steps.title: Five events (Scrum Guide 2020)
steps.body:
- **The Sprint:** fixed length of **one month or less**; container for all other events.
- **Sprint Planning:** max **8 hours** for a one-month Sprint (shorter for shorter Sprints) — why (Sprint Goal), what, how.
- **Daily Scrum:** **15 minutes**, for the Developers, to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan.
- **Sprint Review:** max **4 hours** for a one-month Sprint — inspect the outcome with stakeholders and adapt the Product Backlog (not just a demo).
- **Sprint Retrospective:** max **3 hours** for a one-month Sprint — improve quality and effectiveness.

steps.title: Backlog refinement
steps.body: An **ongoing activity**, not a formal event: breaking down and detailing Product Backlog items so they are ready for future Sprints.

steps.title: Solved example: scale timeboxes
steps.body: Two-week Sprint (half of a month): Sprint Planning is usually shorter than 8 h — many teams use ~4 h. Daily Scrum remains 15 minutes regardless of Sprint length.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Daily Scrum as a status meeting for managers.
- Skipping retrospectives when busy.
- Changing the Sprint Goal mid-Sprint without the Product Owner (only the PO can cancel a Sprint, when the goal becomes obsolete).

steps.title: User stories (a common practice, not required by Scrum)
steps.body:
Format: **As a** [user], **I want** [goal] **so that** [benefit].
Good stories are **INVEST**: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. Add **acceptance criteria**, often as Given/When/Then.

steps.title: Solved example: story + criteria
steps.body:
'As a returning customer, I want to pay with my saved UPI ID so that checkout is faster.'
Given I have a saved UPI ID, when I choose UPI at checkout, then it is pre-filled and I can pay in one tap.

steps.title: Story points and velocity
steps.body:
Many teams estimate relative size in **story points** and track **velocity** = points completed (meeting Definition of Done) per Sprint. Use the **average of recent Sprints** to forecast. Velocity is for the team's planning — not for comparing teams or judging people.
Example: last 3 Sprints = 28, 32, 30 → average **30**. Remaining backlog 150 points → about **5 Sprints**.

steps.title: Kanban basics
steps.body: Visualise work on a board (To do → In progress → Review → Done), **limit work in progress (WIP)**, manage flow, and measure **cycle time**. Little's Law: average cycle time ≈ WIP ÷ throughput. Example: WIP 12 items, throughput 4 items/day → ~3 days cycle time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Converting story points to hours.
- Counting partially done stories in velocity.
- No WIP limits → everything 'in progress', nothing done.
